## Security during the session

A remote session is privileged access, so treat it with care:

- **Verify identity** — confirm you are helping the right person.
- **Never ask for their password** out loud or in chat; you should not need it.
- **Keep the user present and aware** of what you are doing.
- **Avoid opening personal files** or anything unrelated to the issue.
- **End the session cleanly** and confirm the disconnect, so no access lingers.

These habits protect the user, protect you, and keep an auditable, professional standard.

## Your task

Write the spoken script you would use to start a remote-control session with a nervous, non-technical user who is reluctant to let you connect. Include: how you ask for consent, how you reassure them they stay in control, one security point you make, and how you tell them the session has ended at the close. Keep it warm and jargon-free.

hd4-l09-active-directory-identity-basics.title: Active Directory and identity basics
objectives: Explain what Active Directory is and the role of a domain
Describe users, groups, and organizational units (OUs)
Reset a password and unlock an account the correct way
Use group membership to grant access instead of per-user permissions
Verify a caller's identity before making account changes
Handle a realistic account-related ticket end to end
hd4-l09-active-directory-identity-basics.body:
## Why identity is the helpdesk's bread and butter

A huge share of helpdesk tickets are about **identity**: "I can't log in," "my account's locked," "I need access to the shared folder." Behind most of these in a Windows environment sits **Active Directory**. Understanding it turns these tickets from mysteries into routine, confident fixes.

## What Active Directory is

**Active Directory (AD)** is Microsoft's **directory service** — a central database of every **user**, **computer**, and **resource** on a Windows network, plus the rules about who can access what. A network managed this way is called a **domain**. When a user logs into their work PC, the PC asks a **domain controller** (a server running AD) to confirm the password. That single sign-in then governs their access across the network.

## Users, groups, and OUs

Three objects matter most to you:

- A **user account** represents a person and holds their sign-in name and settings.
- A **group** is a collection of users; you grant access to the *group*, and membership grants it to each person.
- An **organizational unit (OU)** is a container that organises users and computers, often by department or site, so policies and admin can be targeted.

```text
Domain: contoso.local
  OU: Finance
    User: sam.patel
    Group: Finance-Share-RW  (members get write access to S:)
```

## Use groups, not per-user permissions

The golden rule of access: **grant through groups**, not to individuals. If Sam needs the finance drive, you add Sam to the **Finance-Share-RW** group — you do *not* edit the drive's permissions for Sam personally. When Sam later moves teams, you remove one group membership and all the right access changes at once. This is **role-based** thinking, and it scales.

## The two everyday fixes

Most identity tickets are one of two things, and they are *not* the same:

- **Account locked** — too many wrong passwords triggered a lockout. The fix is to **unlock** it; the password is fine.
- **Forgotten / expired password** — the fix is a **password reset**, after which the user usually sets a new one at next sign-in.

Diagnosing which one you are dealing with saves time and avoids unnecessary resets.

## Verify identity first — every time

The helpdesk is a favourite target for **social engineering**: an attacker phones pretending to be an employee to get a password reset and seize the account. So before *any* account change, **verify the caller's identity** using your organisation's policy — a callback number, employee ID, security questions, or a manager's confirmation.

```text
"Before I reset that, I need to verify your identity per policy.
Can you confirm your employee ID and the answer to your
security question, please?"
```

This is not bureaucracy. It is one of the most important security controls you personally operate.

## Your task

Write out how you would handle this ticket end to end: "Hi, I'm locked out of my computer and I have a meeting in ten minutes — can you reset my password?" In order, write: the identity-verification step (what you ask and why), how you decide whether it is a lockout or a true password reset, the action you take, and your closing line confirming the fix and any next step for the user.

hd4-l10-lab-day-in-the-life.title: Lab: a day in the life of a helpdesk technician
objectives: Triage and prioritise a realistic mixed ticket queue under time pressure
Classify each contact as incident, request, problem, or change
Apply the six-step troubleshooting method to a live ticket
Communicate with empathy and verify identity where required
Escalate a ticket with a complete, professional handover
Document a worked ticket to a knowledge-base standard
hd4-l10-lab-day-in-the-life.body:
## The shift begins

This lab pulls the whole month together. You are starting an 09:00 shift on a busy service desk. Five tickets are already in your queue. Nothing here is new — but for the first time you must use *all* your skills at once: prioritise, classify, troubleshoot, communicate, escalate, and document. That integration *is* the job.

## Your 09:00 queue

```text
#1  INC: "Whole call centre lost their phones 2 minutes ago." (40 users)
#2  REQ: "Please install Adobe Acrobat on my laptop." (1 user)
#3  INC: "My monitor flickers occasionally." (1 user)
#4  INC: "I'm locked out and have a client call in 10 min." (1 user)
#5  INC: "Outlook won't send; error 0x800CCC0F." (1 user)
```

## Step 1: Triage the queue

Do not work in arrival order. Score each by **impact** and **urgency**:

| # | Type | Impact | Urgency | Priority |
|---|------|--------|---------|----------|
| 1 | Incident (likely **major**) | High (40) | High | **P1** |
| 4 | Incident | Low (1) | High (deadline) | **P2** |
| 5 | Incident | Low (1) | Medium | P3 |
| 2 | Service request | Low | Low | P4 |
| 3 | Incident | Low | Low | P4 |

Ticket #1 is a probable **major incident** — recognise it, raise the alarm, and get the right people on it *before* you touch anything else. You may own the comms, not the fix.

## Step 2: Work ticket #4 with method and care

The locked-out user is stressed and on a deadline — lead with empathy, then verify identity (it is an account change!), then act.

```text
You: "I can absolutely help with that, and I know the timing is
      tight. Quick security check first, per policy - can you
      confirm your employee ID and security answer? ... Thank you.
      You were locked out from failed sign-ins; I'm unlocking it
      now. Try signing in again for me. ... Working? Brilliant."
```

Notice the order: **empathy -> verify -> diagnose (lockout, not reset) -> act -> confirm with user**.

## Step 3: Escalate ticket #1 cleanly

The phone outage needs the telecoms/network team. Your handover:

```text
Ref: INC0050001 | Priority: P1 (suspected major incident)
Summary: Entire call centre (~40 users) lost desk phones at 09:02.
Impact: Customer calls failing; revenue + SLA impact now.
Tried: confirmed multiple users, network switch reachable by ping,
       no recent change noted in change calendar.
Contact: Floor lead Aisha Bello, ext. 2200.
Escalated to: Telecoms/Network on-call. Comms owner: me.
```

## Step 4: Document and close

When the Outlook ticket (#5) resolves, verify with the user, then write the record:

```text
Symptom: Outlook send failing, error 0x800CCC0F.
Cause:   Outgoing (SMTP) server setting was incorrect after profile reset.
Action:  Corrected SMTP server and port; sent test mail successfully.
Outcome: Verified with user - send/receive working. Resolved.
KB:      Linked to article "Fixing Outlook 0x800CCC0F send errors."
```

## Your task

Work the full queue above as if it were your shift. Produce: (1) your triage table with a priority for all five tickets and one line of justification each; (2) a short worked write-up of ticket #5 through the six-step method; (3) a clean escalation note for ticket #1; and (4) a closing message to the locked-out user in #4. Treat this as your portfolio piece for the month.

hd4-l11-rmm-with-ninjaone.title: RMM with NinjaOne: managing the whole fleet
objectives: Explain what an RMM platform is and the role of the agent
Contrast proactive RMM with reactive one-to-one remote support
'List the core RMM capabilities: monitoring, alerting, patching, scripting, remote access, reporting'
Describe how a Tier 1/2 technician uses NinjaOne day to day
Explain why RMM access is a security-sensitive, high-privilege target
Name common RMM alternatives and how the concepts transfer
hd4-l11-rmm-with-ninjaone.body:
## What RMM actually is

A **Remote Monitoring and Management** tool — RMM for short — is the platform IT teams use to look after *every* computer they are responsible for, all from one screen. You install a small background program called an **agent** on each device, and from then on the RMM can see the machine's health, alert you when something is wrong, install updates, run scripts, and let you remote in — across hundreds or thousands of devices at once.

This is the day-to-day cockpit for support teams in managed service providers (MSPs) and in-house IT departments alike. **NinjaOne** is one of the most popular modern RMM platforms, and it is a great example to learn the concepts on.

## RMM vs. the remote-support tools you already met

In the remote-support lesson you learned to connect *into one machine* when a user asks for help — that is reactive and one-at-a-time. RMM is different: the agents are **always on**, so the platform is **proactive**. It watches the whole fleet and tells you a disk is nearly full *before* the user calls. Remote control is just one feature inside an RMM, not the whole point.

## The core capabilities

- **Monitoring & alerting** — device health, disk space, CPU, memory, services, and custom conditions; you get an alert (or a ticket) when something crosses a threshold.
- **Patch management** — approve and deploy Windows and third-party updates across the fleet on a schedule.
- **Automation & scripting** — run a PowerShell script or a built-in automation against one device or a whole group (e.g. clear temp files, restart a service).
- **Software deployment** — push or update applications remotely.
- **Remote access** — jump onto a device (NinjaOne integrates remote control) without interrupting the user.
- **Inventory & reporting** — a live asset list and reports for audits and reviews.

## A day in NinjaOne for a Tier 1/2 tech

You start at the **dashboard**: red and amber alerts at the top. You triage them — a failed backup here, a low-disk warning there. You open a device, check its health and recent activity, run an automation to free space, and confirm the alert clears. A patch policy flags machines missing this month's updates, so you approve the rollout. Throughout, NinjaOne can raise and update **tickets** automatically, and it integrates with the ticketing systems from the earlier lesson so monitoring and your queue stay in sync.

## Why security matters here

An RMM agent runs with **high privilege** on every endpoint, so the RMM console is a powerful — and attractive — target. Real-world attacks have abused RMM tools to push malware to whole fleets. Treat access seriously: enforce **multi-factor authentication**, give each technician the least privilege they need, and review who can run scripts. The same power that helps you fix 500 machines can harm 500 machines.

## Where it fits among the alternatives

NinjaOne sits alongside tools like **Datto RMM, ConnectWise Automate, Atera and Kaseya**. Microsoft **Intune** (covered next module) overlaps for cloud device management. The concepts transfer: learn one RMM well and you can pick up any of them.

## Your task

Sign up for a free NinjaOne trial or watch a product demo. Find and name these five panels: the **dashboard/alerts**, a **device's health page**, **patch management**, **automations/scripts**, and **remote access**. Write one sentence on how an RMM differs from the remote-support tool you used earlier.

hd5-l01-modern-management-and-intune.title: Modern management and an intro to Microsoft Intune
objectives: Contrast traditional management (AD + Group Policy + imaging) with modern cloud management
Describe what Microsoft Intune is and where it fits in Microsoft Intune Suite and Microsoft 365
Navigate the Microsoft Intune admin center and find devices, apps, and policies
Explain the role of the Intune MDM and how a device 'enrolls'
Identify the difference between MDM and MAM at a high level
Know what an Endpoint Administrator does and how MD-102 maps to the job
hd5-l01-modern-management-and-intune.body:
## From the old world to the cloud

If you have worked Tier 1, you have probably met **traditional management**: a Windows PC joined to an on-premises **Active Directory** domain, pushed settings via **Group Policy**, and built from a hand-crafted **image**. It works, but it assumes the device is on the corporate network and that someone built that image by hand.

**Modern management** flips this. The device is managed from the **cloud**, over the internet, from anywhere. Settings, apps, and security all flow down from a cloud service. This matters enormously for a hybrid and remote workforce — the PC at someone's kitchen table is just as manageable as the one in the office.

## What is Microsoft Intune?

**Microsoft Intune** is Microsoft's cloud service for managing devices and apps. It is the engine of modern management. Intune can manage Windows, macOS, iOS/iPadOS, and Android, and it sits inside the broader **Microsoft 365** and **Microsoft Intune Suite** family alongside Entra ID and Defender.

Intune does the jobs you used to do by hand or with Group Policy: deploy apps, push **configuration profiles**, enforce **compliance**, and apply security baselines — all from one console.

## MDM vs MAM

Two terms you will hear constantly:

- **MDM (Mobile Device Management)** manages the *whole device*. Think company-owned laptops fully enrolled into Intune.
- **MAM (Mobile Application Management)** protects company *data inside apps* without managing the whole device. Think a personal phone where only the Outlook work account is protected.

Knowing which one applies tells you how much control you have and what you can troubleshoot.

## A tour of the admin center

The console you will live in is the **Microsoft Intune admin center**.

```text
1. Go to https://intune.microsoft.com
2. Sign in with an admin account
3. Left menu, explore the key blades:
   - Devices  -> enrolled devices and their state
   - Apps     -> what you deploy to devices
   - Endpoint security -> baselines, antivirus, Defender
   - Reports  -> compliance and deployment status
   - Tenant administration -> connectors and roles
```

Spend time here. Click **Devices**, pick one, and look at its hardware, compliance, and the policies applied to it. This single device blade answers most Tier 2 questions.

## Enrollment in one sentence

**Enrollment** is the moment a device registers with Intune so it can receive policies and report back. No enrollment, no management relationship — so when a policy 'isn't applying', the first question is often: *is the device actually enrolled and checking in?*

## The role and the exam

The job title is **Endpoint Administrator**, and the certification that maps to it is **MD-102**. As you move from Tier 1 to Tier 2, you stop just resetting passwords and start owning device configuration, app delivery, and compliance. This month builds exactly those skills.

## Your task

Sign in to the Microsoft Intune admin center, open the **Devices** blade, pick any enrolled device, and write down three facts about it: its compliance state, its operating system version, and one policy applied to it.

hd5-l02-entra-id-and-device-identity.title: Entra ID and device identity (join types)
objectives: Explain what Microsoft Entra ID is and how it relates to the former Azure AD
Describe the three device identity join types and when each is used
Use dsregcmd /status on Windows to read a device's join state
Locate and interpret device join type in the Entra admin center and Intune
Explain at a high level what a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is and why it matters
Decide how join type affects sign-in, policy, and the tickets you can resolve
hd5-l02-entra-id-and-device-identity.body:
## What Microsoft Entra ID is

**Microsoft Entra ID** is Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service - it is the product formerly called **Azure Active Directory (Azure AD)**. The rename is just branding; the tenant, accounts, groups, and tokens are the same. Entra ID is where user accounts live, where sign-ins are authenticated, and where **Conditional Access** policies decide whether a sign-in is allowed. For helpdesk work, the key shift from classic on-prem **Active Directory (AD)** is that identity now lives in the cloud and devices can register themselves with that cloud directory.

A **device identity** is simply a record of a device in Entra ID. Having that record lets you target the device with policy, see it in reports, and let **Conditional Access** require a managed or compliant device before granting access.

## The three join types

There are three ways a Windows device can have an identity in Entra ID:

- **Entra registered** - the device is personal (BYOD). The user adds their work account, but the device itself is owned by the person. Used for phones, home PCs, and contractor laptops. You get limited management.
- **Entra joined** - the device is corporate-owned and **cloud-only**. It is joined directly to Entra ID with no on-prem AD involvement. This is the modern target state, usually managed by **Intune**.
- **Entra hybrid joined** - the device is joined to **both** on-prem AD and Entra ID. This is common in organizations still migrating to the cloud that need **Group Policy** and on-prem resources while also using Entra and Intune.

A quick rule of thumb: personal = registered, cloud-only corporate = joined, still tied to on-prem AD = hybrid joined.

## The Primary Refresh Token (PRT)

When a user signs in on an Entra joined or hybrid joined device, Entra issues a **Primary Refresh Token (PRT)**. At a high level the PRT proves "this user, on this device," and lets the device silently get tokens for apps and websites without re-prompting. That is what powers **single sign-on (SSO)**. If SSO suddenly breaks across many apps, a broken or missing PRT is a prime suspect.

## Checking join type on the device

The fastest check on Windows is **dsregcmd**:

```text
Open a Command Prompt and run:
dsregcmd /status
```

```powershell
# Read the Device State section of the output:
# AzureAdJoined : YES   -> registered in Entra
# EnterpriseJoined : NO
# DomainJoined : YES    -> also joined to on-prem AD
# If AzureAdJoined=YES and DomainJoined=NO  -> Entra joined (cloud-only)
# If AzureAdJoined=YES and DomainJoined=YES -> Entra hybrid joined
# AzureAdPrt : YES      -> a Primary Refresh Token is present
```

## Checking join type in the portal

You can confirm the same thing from the cloud side:

```text
Entra admin center (entra.microsoft.com)
> Devices > All devices
> select the device
> read the "Join type" column / property: Entra registered, Entra joined, or Entra hybrid joined
```

The same devices appear in **Intune** under Devices, where you can also see compliance and assigned policies. Join type affects what you can fix: a **registered** BYOD device gives you little control, while an Entra **joined** device managed by Intune lets you push policy, wipe, or reset.

## Your task

On a Windows device, run `dsregcmd /status` and identify the join type from the AzureAdJoined and DomainJoined values, and confirm whether AzureAdPrt is YES. Then open the Entra admin center, go to Devices > All devices, find that same device, and confirm its Join type matches what the command reported. Write one sentence explaining how that join type would affect a sign-in troubleshooting ticket.

hd5-l03-windows-autopilot.title: Windows Autopilot deployment
objectives: Explain what Windows Autopilot is and how it removes the need for imaging
Describe how a device is registered using its hardware hash
Configure and assign a Windows Autopilot deployment profile
Compare user-driven and self-deploying deployment modes
Explain the purpose of the Enrollment Status Page (ESP) during OOBE
Walk through the Autopilot screens in the Intune admin center
hd5-l03-windows-autopilot.body:
## What Windows Autopilot is

**Windows Autopilot** is a cloud-driven way to set up and configure brand-new Windows devices. The goal is **zero-touch provisioning**: a device ships from the factory with a standard Windows install, and when the user turns it on and connects to the internet, it automatically becomes a fully configured, corporate-ready PC - joined to **Entra ID**, enrolled in **Intune**, with policies and apps applied. The technician never touches the box.

The big win for helpdesk teams is the end of **imaging**. Traditionally you built a custom Windows image, stored it, and applied it to every machine - slow, version-sensitive work. With Autopilot you start from the OEM's factory OS and let the cloud do the configuration. Less time per device, fewer images to maintain, and devices can be drop-shipped straight to users.

## Registering a device (hardware hash)

For Autopilot to recognize a device, that device must be **registered** to your tenant. Registration is keyed on the **hardware hash** (also called the hardware ID) - a value derived from the device's hardware. There are three common ways it gets registered:

- The **OEM or reseller** registers it at purchase (the smoothest path).
- You **collect the hash** from an existing device and import it.
- A **distributor** uploads it on your behalf.

To collect the hash yourself from a device:

```powershell
# Run in an elevated PowerShell session
Install-Script -Name Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo -Force
Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo -OutputFile C:\HWID\AutopilotHWID.csv
```

You then import that CSV into Intune so the device shows up as an Autopilot device.

## Deployment profiles

A **deployment profile** is the set of rules that tells Autopilot how to configure a device: which **join type** (Entra joined or hybrid joined), what the out-of-box experience should hide or show, the naming convention, and which mode to use. You build the profile once and **assign** it to a group; any registered device in that group picks it up automatically.

## User-driven vs self-deploying modes

There are two main modes:

- **User-driven** - the end user signs in with their **work account** during setup. The device is provisioned and assigned to that user. This is the common choice for normal staff laptops.
- **Self-deploying** - **no user signs in**. The device provisions itself end-to-end. This is for **kiosks, digital signage, and shared devices** where there is no single owner.

## OOBE and the Enrollment Status Page

When the device first boots, the user sees the **Out-of-Box Experience (OOBE)** - the standard Windows setup screens. Autopilot customizes OOBE based on the profile, then hands off to the **Enrollment Status Page (ESP)**. The ESP shows provisioning **progress** and can **block** the user from reaching the desktop until required apps, certificates, and policies are installed - so users don't start working on a half-configured machine.

```text
Intune admin center (intune.microsoft.com)
> Devices > Enrollment > Windows
> Windows Autopilot:  Devices  |  Deployment profiles  |  Enrollment Status Page
```

From here you confirm a device is registered, create or edit a deployment profile, assign it to a group, and configure the ESP behavior.

## Your task

In the Intune admin center, navigate to Devices > Enrollment > Windows and open the Windows Autopilot area. Review the Devices, Deployment profiles, and Enrollment Status Page sections. Then describe, in three to four sentences, how you would take a brand-new laptop from its box to a user's hands using Autopilot - name the hardware hash registration step, the deployment profile, the mode you would choose (user-driven), and the role the ESP plays during OOBE.

hd5-l04-app-deployment-with-intune.title: App deployment and management with Intune
objectives: 'Identify the main app types Intune can deploy: Win32, line-of-business, Microsoft Store, web link,
hd5-l04-app-deployment-with-intune.body:
## Why app delivery matters

A huge slice of Tier 1 and Tier 2 work is getting the right software onto the right machine. With **Microsoft Intune** you stop walking USB sticks to desks and instead push apps from the cloud to enrolled Windows devices. Intune downloads the package, runs the installer silently, checks whether it worked, and reports status back to the admin center. Understanding this pipeline lets you move from "it won't install" tickets to confidently diagnosing the cause.

## App types in Intune

Intune supports several app types, each suited to a different source:

- **Win32 app** — your custom EXE, MSI, or script installers, packaged into a **.intunewin** file. This is the workhorse for in-house and third-party software.
- **Line-of-business (LOB) app** — a single MSI you upload directly, simpler but less flexible than Win32.
- **Microsoft Store app** — apps pulled from the new Microsoft Store integration; Intune handles updates automatically.
- **Web link** — a shortcut to a web app that appears in the Company Portal.
- **Microsoft 365 Apps** — a guided way to deploy Office (Word, Excel, Outlook) with channel and language options.

## Packaging a Win32 app

Win32 apps must be wrapped first. The **Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool** (`IntuneWinAppUtil.exe`) takes your source folder and setup file and produces one encrypted `.intunewin` package.

```powershell
IntuneWinAppUtil.exe -c C:\Source -s setup.exe -o C:\Output
```

You then upload that `.intunewin`, specify the silent **install and uninstall commands**, and define a **detection rule** so Intune knows when the app is present.

## Assigning apps

Adding an app does nothing until you assign it. There are three intents:

- **Required** — Intune force-installs the app automatically.
- **Available for enrolled devices** — the app appears in the **Company Portal** for users to install on demand.
- **Uninstall** — Intune removes the app from targeted devices.

You assign to **Microsoft Entra groups**. A key decision is **user groups versus device groups**: assign to a *user* group when the app should follow the person (Available apps usually target users); assign to a *device* group when the software must be on the machine no matter who logs in, such as a security agent.

```text
Intune admin center (intune.microsoft.com)
  > Apps > Windows > + Add
  > pick app type > upload package and set install/detect rules
  > Assignments > add group under Required / Available / Uninstall
```

## How status is reported

The **Company Portal** app is the user-facing storefront for Available apps and shows install progress. On the admin side, each app's **Device install status** and **User install status** pages report Installed, Failed, or Not applicable, along with an error code. The **detection rule** is what decides "Installed," so a mismatched rule is a frequent cause of phantom failures.

## Troubleshooting failures

When an app shows **Failed**, work through the basics: confirm the device has synced (it must check in to receive the assignment), verify the **install command line** is correct and silent, check for missing **dependencies**, and re-examine the **detection rule** to be sure it matches what the installer actually drops. Error codes from the status pages map to specific failures.

## Your task

In a test tenant, package a small free tool (for example, 7-Zip) into a `.intunewin` file with the Content Prep Tool, upload it as a Win32 app, set a detection rule, assign it as **Available** to a test user group, and confirm it appears in the Company Portal. Then add a second assignment as **Required** to a device group and verify the install status reports correctly.

hd5-l05-configuration-and-compliance-pol.title: Configuration profiles and compliance policies
objectives: Explain the difference between a configuration profile (sets settings) and a compliance policy (checks
hd5-l05-configuration-and-compliance-pol.body:
## Two jobs: setting versus checking

The single most important idea in this lesson is the difference between **configuration** and **compliance**. A **configuration profile** *sets* something on a device: it pushes and enforces settings like a Wi-Fi profile, a VPN connection, or a screen-lock timeout. A **compliance policy** *checks* something: it evaluates a device against rules and reports whether the device is **compliant** or **non-compliant**. Configuration changes the device; compliance only judges it. Keeping that distinction clear will save you on the MD-102 exam and on the job.

## Configuration profiles

When you need a setting applied everywhere, you create a **configuration profile**. Intune offers a few ways to author them:

- **Settings catalog** — a searchable list of thousands of individual settings you pick from; this is the modern, preferred approach.
- **Templates** — pre-grouped profiles for common scenarios like VPN, Wi-Fi, email, or endpoint protection.
- **Administrative templates** — the cloud answer to on-premises **Group Policy**, exposing familiar ADMX-style settings for admins coming from Active Directory.

```text
Intune admin center (intune.microsoft.com)
  > Devices > Configuration > + Create > New Policy
  > pick platform (Windows) and Settings catalog or Templates
  > add settings > Assignments > choose groups
```

The profile is then assigned to **Microsoft Entra groups** of users or devices, just like apps.

## Compliance policies

A **compliance policy** is a set of rules a device must satisfy. Typical rules include **BitLocker required**, a **minimum OS version**, **password required**, and Microsoft Defender being healthy. Intune evaluates the device against these rules on a schedule and stamps it **Compliant** or **Not compliant**. Crucially, compliance does *not* fix anything; it reports. If you want BitLocker actually turned on, that is a *configuration* job.

```text
Intune admin center (intune.microsoft.com)
  > Devices > Compliance > + Create policy
  > choose platform > define rules (BitLocker, min OS, password)
  > Actions for noncompliance > set grace period
  > Assignments > choose groups
```

## Actions and grace periods

Under **Actions for noncompliance** you decide what happens when a device fails. Options include sending the user an email, marking the device non-compliant after a delay, or remotely locking it. A **grace period** delays the non-compliant mark for a number of days, giving the user time to remediate before they lose access. This softens enforcement and cuts down on sudden lockout tickets.

## Compliance meets Conditional Access

Compliance becomes powerful when it feeds **Conditional Access**. A Conditional Access policy in Microsoft Entra can require that a device be **marked compliant** before it is allowed to reach resources like Exchange Online or SharePoint. So if a laptop fails its compliance policy, Conditional Access can **block** it from corporate email until it is fixed. This is how the two halves connect: compliance produces a verdict, and Conditional Access acts on it.

## Putting it together

In practice you usually pair them: a configuration profile *enables* BitLocker and sets a password policy, while a compliance policy *verifies* those same controls and reports to Conditional Access. One enforces, the other audits, and together they keep only healthy devices on the network.

## Your task

In a test tenant, create a Windows **configuration profile** using the settings catalog that sets a screen-lock timeout, and assign it to a test group. Then create a **compliance policy** that requires BitLocker and a minimum OS version, configure an action for noncompliance with a short **grace period**, assign it, and describe in one or two sentences how a Conditional Access policy could use that compliance state to block a non-compliant device from email.

hd5-l06-endpoint-security-and-defender.title: Endpoint security and Microsoft Defender
objectives: Navigate the Endpoint security node in the Microsoft Intune admin center
Explain what a security baseline is and why it speeds up secure configuration
Configure Microsoft Defender Antivirus, firewall, and BitLocker disk encryption policies
Describe attack surface reduction (ASR) rules and what they block
Explain the difference between antivirus (prevention) and EDR (detection and response)
Connect Intune with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint so device risk drives compliance
hd5-l06-endpoint-security-and-defender.body:
## The Endpoint security node

Inside the **Microsoft Intune admin center** there is a section built just for hardening devices: the **Endpoint security** node. This is where an Endpoint Administrator lives when the job is *security* rather than general configuration. From here you deploy **security baselines**, antivirus policy, firewall rules, disk encryption, and **attack surface reduction** rules, and you connect to Microsoft Defender.

```text
1. Go to https://intune.microsoft.com
2. Left menu -> Endpoint security
3. Browse the categories:
   - Security baselines
   - Antivirus
   - Disk encryption (BitLocker)
   - Firewall
   - Attack surface reduction
   - Endpoint detection and response
```

## Security baselines

There are hundreds of security settings in Windows. A **security baseline** is a Microsoft-recommended, pre-configured *group* of those settings, so instead of choosing each one by hand you deploy a hardened starting point and then tweak. Baselines exist for Windows, Microsoft Edge, and Defender for Endpoint. Deploy one to a pilot group first, review what it changes, then widen the rollout.

## Defender Antivirus, firewall and BitLocker

Three everyday protections you configure here:

- **Microsoft Defender Antivirus** — real-time protection, cloud-delivered protection, and scheduled scans. This is built into Windows; you are tuning policy, not installing software.
- **Firewall** — control inbound and outbound traffic per profile (domain, private, public).
- **Disk encryption (BitLocker)** — encrypt the system drive so a lost laptop does not leak data, with recovery keys escrowed to Entra ID.

These map directly to common Tier 2 tickets: "why is this site blocked", "where is my BitLocker recovery key", "why did a scan quarantine a file".

## Attack surface reduction

**Attack surface reduction (ASR)** rules block the *behaviours* attackers rely on, things legitimate software rarely needs. Examples: stopping Office apps from spawning child processes, blocking untrusted or unsigned scripts, and blocking credential theft from LSASS. You can run a rule in **audit** mode first to see what it *would* block before enforcing it, which avoids breaking a line-of-business app.

## Antivirus versus EDR

This distinction matters for the exam and the job. **Antivirus** is *prevention*: it stops and removes *known* malware. **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint** adds **EDR** — *Endpoint Detection and Response* — which watches device behaviour, raises **alerts** and groups them into **incidents**, and lets you investigate and respond (isolate a device, collect a forensic package). Prevention catches the known; EDR catches the sneaky and the new.

You review all of this in the **Microsoft Defender portal** at **security.microsoft.com**: the incident queue, device risk levels, and recommended actions.

## Connecting Intune and Defender for Endpoint

The two services are stronger together. When you wire up the **Microsoft Defender for Endpoint connector** in Intune, each device's **risk score** flows back into Intune. A **compliance policy** can then say "a device at high risk is non-compliant", and **Conditional Access** can block that device from company data until it is cleaned up, no manual checking required.

## Your task

Open **Endpoint security** in the Intune admin center. Open the **Security baselines** category and note which baselines are available. Then open **Attack surface reduction** and write down two ASR rules and, in your own words, what behaviour each one blocks.

hd5-l07-windows-update-for-business.title: Windows Update for Business and patching
objectives: Explain how Windows Update for Business patches devices without WSUS
Configure update rings in Intune using deferral, deadline and active hours settings
Distinguish feature updates from quality updates and manage each
Describe how to expedite an update for a zero-day or critical fix
Pause, resume, and roll back updates when a patch causes problems
Monitor update compliance using Intune reports, and explain Windows Autopatch at a high level
hd5-l07-windows-update-for-business.body:
## Patching without WSUS

In the old world, patches flowed through an on-prem **WSUS** server: you stored updates locally, approved each one, and pushed them to domain-joined PCs. Modern management does it differently. With **Windows Update for Business (WUfB)**, devices download updates *directly from Microsoft's cloud*, and you simply set **policy** in Intune to control *when* and *how* they install. No WSUS server, no approvals queue, and it works for the remote laptop just as well as the office desktop.

## Update rings

The core tool is the **update ring**. A ring is a policy you target at a group of devices that controls update timing. The key settings:

- **Deferral** — how many days to wait after Microsoft releases an update before this group installs it.
- **Deadline** — the point after which the update is forced and the device will restart, even if the user keeps postponing.
- **Active hours** — the daily window when restarts are *not* allowed, so a reboot never interrupts someone mid-meeting.

```text
1. Go to https://intune.microsoft.com
2. Devices -> Windows -> Update rings for Windows 10 and later
3. Create policy, set deferral, deadline, active hours
4. Assign it to a device group (start with a pilot ring)
```

A typical strategy uses several rings: a small **pilot** ring with short deferral, then **broad** and **critical** rings with longer deferral. If a patch breaks the pilot, you find out before it reaches everyone.

## Feature updates vs quality updates

Two kinds of update, managed separately:

- **Quality updates** — the smaller, monthly **cumulative** security and reliability fixes (the classic "Patch Tuesday").
- **Feature updates** — the larger, roughly annual upgrades that move a device to a new Windows version (for example 23H2 to 24H2). In Intune you create a **Feature updates** policy to pin or advance the target version, so you decide when the big jump happens.

## Why deferral and deadlines reduce risk

It is a balancing act. Patch too fast and a flawed update can take out your whole fleet; patch too slowly and you leave known vulnerabilities open. **Deferral** plus a **ring strategy** lets a pilot group absorb the risk first, while **deadlines** guarantee devices don't drift unpatched forever and **active hours** keep restarts out of the working day. Security and stability, both protected.

## Expedite, pause and roll back

Sometimes the normal schedule is too slow. For a **zero-day** or critical fix you can **expedite** an update, pushing it within hours and bypassing the configured deferral. Conversely, if a patch causes problems you can **pause** updates for a ring to stop the bleeding, and for quality updates you can **roll back** (uninstall) the latest update while you investigate.

## Monitoring and Windows Autopatch

Deploying isn't enough, you must confirm devices actually patched. Intune provides **Windows update reports** showing compliance, failures, and which version each device is on, your evidence that the fleet is current. For teams that want this run *for* them, **Windows Autopatch** is a managed Microsoft service that automatically groups devices into rings and orchestrates Windows, Office, Edge, and driver updates, a hands-off option built on the same WUfB foundations.

## Your task

In the Intune admin center, go to **Devices > Windows > Update rings**. Open (or create) an update ring and write down its **deferral**, **deadline**, and **active hours** values. Then, in your own words, explain how those three settings together protect both security and the user experience.

hd5-l08-ai-tools-for-support.title: AI tools for support: Copilot and AI ticket triage
objectives: Describe Microsoft Copilot and its key variants (Copilot chat, Copilot in Intune, Microsoft Security
hd5-l08-ai-tools-for-support.body:
## What is Microsoft Copilot?

**Microsoft Copilot** is Microsoft's family of generative AI assistants built into the tools you already use. For a support tech, three variants matter most. **Copilot chat** (the general assistant in Microsoft 365, Edge, and Windows) helps you summarize, draft, and reason in plain language. **Copilot in Intune** is embedded in the Intune admin center and can answer natural-language questions about *your tenant's own* devices, policies, and apps. **Microsoft Security Copilot** is the security-operations assistant that helps SOC teams investigate incidents and alerts.

You will also meet general LLM assistants (the public chatbots). They are powerful for drafting and explaining, but they do **not** see your tenant data and they carry real privacy and accuracy risks.

## Triage: from chaos to a sorted queue

Tier 1 lives in the ticket queue. AI shines at the boring-but-critical triage work: reading a long thread, pulling out what matters, and suggesting where the ticket should go. Use it to **summarize** a 40-message email chain into three lines, **classify** a ticket by category, and **suggest a priority** and routing queue.

```text
Summarize this ticket thread in 4 bullets: the user's core problem,
what has already been tried, the current state, and the single most
likely next step. Then suggest a category (hardware / network /
identity / app) and a priority (P1-P4) with a one-line reason.
[paste thread]
```

## Turning a vague report into structured steps

Users rarely write good tickets. "My laptop is broken" is a starting point, not a diagnosis. Ask AI to convert the vague report into structured clarifying questions and a ranked list of likely causes plus the first diagnostic step for each.

```text
A user reports: "Outlook keeps asking me to sign in and then fails."
List the 5 most likely causes ranked by probability for a Microsoft
365 / Entra ID managed device, the one question I should ask the user
for each, and the first thing I should check. Keep it concise.
```

## Drafting replies and finding KB articles

AI is great at drafting a **clear, friendly, professional reply** at the right reading level. It can also suggest which **KB articles** likely apply. But you are accountable for what you send.

```text
Draft a short, friendly reply telling the user we have reset their
password, they must change it at next sign-in, and to call us if MFA
fails. Plain English, no jargon, under 80 words.
```

## Copilot in Intune: ask your tenant

Inside the Intune admin center you can ask Copilot questions about real devices.

```text
1. Go to https://intune.microsoft.com
2. Open a device or a policy blade
3. Open the Copilot pane
4. Ask: "Why is this device showing as non-compliant?"
   or "Which policies are assigned to this device?"
```

This grounds the answer in *your* data rather than the open internet, which makes it far more trustworthy than a public chatbot for tenant questions.

## Verify before you trust

This is the rule that separates a pro from a liability. **AI can hallucinate** — it can invent facts, KB numbers, and error-code meanings with total confidence. So: never send an AI reply blindly; read every line and confirm the facts. Watch for **PII and secrets** — never paste passwords, tokens, customer data, or internal IPs into a public LLM. Cross-check any technical claim against **official Microsoft docs**. AI gives you a faster first draft and a set of hypotheses, not the final word.

## Your task

Take one real (or realistic) messy ticket thread. Use an AI assistant to (1) summarize it in four bullets, (2) suggest a category and priority, and (3) draft a user reply. Then edit the reply for accuracy and tone, and write one sentence on what you had to correct.

hd5-l09-resolving-endpoint-problems-with.title: Resolving modern endpoint problems with AI
objectives: 'Gather the right diagnostic signal before asking AI: error codes, logs, Event Viewer, and IntuneManagementExtension
hd5-l09-resolving-endpoint-problems-with.body:
## The diagnostic loop

Modern endpoint problems are rarely solved by guessing. The reliable pattern is a loop: **gather signal**, **feed structured context to AI**, **ask for ranked hypotheses and the next step**, then **validate** against the portal and Microsoft Learn. AI is a thinking partner that points you at likely causes fast — it is not the source of truth. You are.

## Step 1: gather the signal

AI is only as good as the context you give it. Before you prompt anything, collect concrete evidence. On a Windows endpoint that means:

```text
- The exact error code (e.g. 0x80180014-style hex codes)
- Event Viewer: Applications and Services Logs >
  Microsoft > Windows > DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics
- The IntuneManagementExtension log (for Win32 apps + PS scripts):
  C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\IntuneManagementExtension\Logs
- The device's compliance, sync, and policy state in Intune
```

A vague "it won't enroll" becomes a solvable problem the moment you have the error code and the relevant log lines.

## Step 2: feed structured context to AI

Give the AI the facts, then ask for *ranked hypotheses* and the single next diagnostic step — not a magic fix.

```text
A Windows 11 device fails Intune enrollment with error 0x80180014.
Context: Entra hybrid-joined, user is licensed, MDM auto-enrollment
is configured. Give me the 4 most likely causes ranked by
probability, the one log or setting to check for each, and the
first diagnostic step. Note any cause you are unsure about.
```

That "note any cause you are unsure about" line is gold — it nudges the model to flag its own uncertainty.

## Step 3: use Copilot in Intune for real device state

For anything tenant-specific, **Copilot in Intune** beats a public chatbot because it reads your real data.

```text
1. Go to https://intune.microsoft.com
2. Devices > pick the affected device
3. Open the Copilot pane and ask:
   "Why is this device non-compliant and what policy is failing?"
   "When did this device last check in, and is it syncing?"
```

## Common problems AI helps with

- **Enrollment failures** — licensing, auto-enrollment scope, device limits, or hybrid-join trust issues.
- **Sync / check-in stalls** — the device hasn't talked to Intune; policies look 'not applied' because nothing has run yet.
- **Compliance gone red** — a single setting (BitLocker, Defender, OS version) flipped the device non-compliant, which can then trigger a **Conditional Access** lockout.
- **App install failures** — Win32 app detection rules, dependencies, or requirement rules; the IME log holds the real reason.
- **BitLocker / Conditional Access lockouts** — escalate carefully; AI helps you read the policy chain, but never bypass security controls on a hunch.

## Verify, always

Here is the discipline that keeps you safe. **AI gives hypotheses, not gospel.** It can confidently invent the meaning of an error code that does not exist. So validate every code and claim against **official Microsoft Learn docs** and confirm the actual state in the **portal and logs** before you act. Cross-check the IME log against what the AI claimed. And never paste secrets, tokens, or user PII into a public LLM — strip identifiers first. The AI narrows your search; the evidence closes the case.

## Your task

Pick a real or simulated endpoint issue (an app that won't install or a device gone non-compliant). Collect the error code and one log excerpt, write a structured prompt asking for ranked hypotheses, then validate the top hypothesis in the Intune portal or against Microsoft Learn. Write down which hypothesis was correct and how you confirmed it.

hd5-l10-ai-assisted-scripting.title: AI-assisted scripting and automation
objectives: Use AI to generate and explain PowerShell for endpoint tasks like Graph queries and bulk operations
Write effective prompts that state the goal, environment, modules, constraints, and error handling
Generate Intune remediation script pairs (detection + remediation) with AI as a starting point
Always request -WhatIf, confirmation prompts, and safe defaults for any destructive operation
'Verify AI-generated scripts: read every line, check cmdlet and parameter names, and confirm Graph scopes'
'Apply safe practice: test on a pilot device, keep secrets out of prompts, and version-control and peer-review
hd5-l10-ai-assisted-scripting.body:
## Why AI is great at PowerShell (and where it bites)

PowerShell is the automation language of endpoint management, and AI is a genuinely strong pair-programmer for it. It can draft a **Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK** query, scaffold a bulk device operation, write an Intune **remediation script pair**, or explain a script you inherited line by line. The catch: AI also **hallucinates cmdlet and parameter names**, invents Graph scopes, and will happily write destructive code with a straight face. Treated as a fast first draft you fully verify, it is a superpower. Treated as an oracle, it is a production incident waiting to happen.

## Prompt patterns that produce good scripts

Vague prompts produce vague, risky code. State the **goal**, the **environment and modules**, the **constraints**, and the **error handling** you expect.

```text
Write a PowerShell script using the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK
to list all Intune-managed Windows devices that haven't checked in
for 30+ days. Requirements: use Connect-MgGraph with least-privilege
scopes, add error handling, include -WhatIf-safe read-only calls,
comment every step, and tell me exactly which Graph scopes are
needed. Do not include any secrets; use placeholders.
```

Asking it to *name the required scopes* and *comment every step* turns the output into something you can actually review.

## A sample generated snippet

Here is the kind of read-only output you might get — and must still read carefully:

```powershell
# Requires: Microsoft.Graph module
# Scopes needed: DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All"

$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All |
  Where-Object { $_.LastSyncDateTime -lt $cutoff } |
  Select-Object DeviceName, UserPrincipalName, LastSyncDateTime |
  Sort-Object LastSyncDateTime
```

Before trusting it: does `Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice` actually exist with those parameters? Is the property name `LastSyncDateTime` correct? Check the docs — do not assume.

## Remediation script pairs

Intune **remediations** use a **detection** script (exit 1 if the issue is present) plus a **remediation** script (the fix). AI is great for scaffolding both, but a remediation runs on real machines, so safety matters double.

```text
Generate an Intune remediation pair in PowerShell: detection checks
if a registry value HKLM:\...\Foo equals 1; remediation sets it to 1.
Follow Intune exit-code conventions, add error handling, log to a
file, and make the remediation idempotent. Comment every line.
```

## Verify before you run — non-negotiable

This is the most important section of the lesson. **Never run AI-generated scripts in production untested.** The rules:

- **Read every line** and understand what it does. If you can't explain it, you can't run it.
- **Check cmdlet and parameter names** against official docs — AI invents plausible-looking ones.
- **Run `-WhatIf` first** and add confirmation prompts on any destructive cmdlet (`Remove-*`, `Set-*`, `Disable-*`).
- **Test on one pilot device or a tiny pilot group**, never the whole fleet.
- **Verify Graph permission scopes** — least privilege, not the broadest scope the AI grabbed.
- **Review for destructive operations** hidden in the middle of innocent-looking code.
- **Keep secrets and PII out of prompts** — use placeholders for tenant IDs, UPNs, and never paste client secrets.
- **Version-control and peer-review** every script before it goes near production.

## Your task

Use an AI assistant to generate one read-only Microsoft Graph PowerShell script (for example: list devices not checked in for 30 days). Then audit it: confirm every cmdlet and parameter exists in the official docs, identify the Graph scopes it needs, and write two sentences on anything the AI got wrong or that you had to change before you would run it.

hd6-l01-m365-tenant-overview.title: Microsoft 365 tenant overview
objectives: Explain what a Microsoft 365 tenant is and how it maps to a single organisation
Navigate the Microsoft 365 admin center and the specialist admin centers
Describe how licensing and subscriptions assign capabilities to users
Identify where domains, DNS, and Microsoft Entra ID fit into a tenant
Use admin roles to control who can change tenant settings
Locate the tenant ID and key settings needed to support and audit a tenant
hd6-l01-m365-tenant-overview.body:
## What a tenant really is

When an organisation buys Microsoft 365, Microsoft creates a **tenant** for them: a dedicated, logically isolated instance of all the cloud services — identity, email, Teams, SharePoint, security tooling — that belongs only to that organisation. Your company's tenant is separate from every other company's, even though they all run on the same Microsoft cloud.

Every tenant has a unique **tenant ID** (a GUID) and a default domain in the form `yourcompany.onmicrosoft.com`. As a Tier 2 admin, the tenant is the boundary you work inside all day.

## The admin centers

You manage the tenant through a set of web portals. The hub is the **Microsoft 365 admin center** at `admin.microsoft.com`, where you handle users, groups, licences, and service health, and from which you jump to the specialist portals.

```text
Microsoft 365 admin center (admin.microsoft.com)
  +-- Exchange admin center        (email)
  +-- Teams admin center           (meetings, calling)
  +-- SharePoint admin center      (sites, OneDrive)
  +-- Microsoft Entra admin center (identity)
  +-- Microsoft Purview            (compliance)
  +-- Microsoft Defender portal    (security)
```

Knowing which portal owns which job is half the battle when a ticket lands.

## Identity and domains

Underneath everything sits **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD). It stores user accounts, groups, and the **authentication** that every service trusts. When a user signs in to Outlook, Teams, or SharePoint, Entra ID is what verifies them.

Most organisations add a **custom domain** like `contoso.com` so that sign-in names and email addresses look professional. Adding a domain means verifying ownership through DNS records — typically a TXT record to prove control, then MX and other records so mail flows.

## Licensing: what unlocks what

A tenant subscribes to one or more **plans** (for example Microsoft 365 Business Premium or E3/E5). Each plan is a bundle of **licences** that unlock specific services. You assign licences **per user** — a user with no Exchange licence has no mailbox; a user with no Copilot licence cannot use Copilot.

When a user reports "I can't get to Teams" your first reflex should be to check their assigned licences in the admin center before you touch anything else.

## Roles and least privilege

Not every admin needs full power. **Admin roles** decide who can change what. The **Global Administrator** role can do everything — which is exactly why you give it to very few people. For day-to-day support, narrower roles like **Helpdesk Administrator** (reset passwords) or **User Administrator** (manage users) follow the principle of **least privilege**: grant the smallest role that does the job.

```text
Admin center > Roles > Role assignments
  - Find the role (e.g. Helpdesk Administrator)
  - Assign the specific user
  - Review assignments regularly
```

## Your task

Sign in to a Microsoft 365 admin center (use a free Microsoft 365 Developer tenant if you don't have one). Find and write down your tenant's default `.onmicrosoft.com` domain and tenant ID, list which specialist admin centers you can reach from the hub, and note which admin role you would assign to a Tier 1 colleague who only needs to reset passwords.

hd6-l02-identity-and-access-in-m365.title: Identity and access management in Microsoft 365
objectives: Describe Microsoft Entra ID as the identity layer for Microsoft 365
Tell the difference between cloud-only and synced (hybrid) identities via Entra Connect
Create and manage users and choose between security and Microsoft 365 groups
Assign licences efficiently with group-based licensing
Enable multi-factor authentication and build a basic Conditional Access policy
'Resolve common Tier 2 tasks: password resets, account lockouts, and self-service password reset'
hd6-l02-identity-and-access-in-m365.body:
## Entra ID: the identity layer behind Microsoft 365

Every time someone signs in to Outlook, Teams, or SharePoint, they authenticate against **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure Active Directory). Entra ID is the **identity and access management** service for the whole tenant. It stores users and groups, checks passwords and other factors, and decides what each person is allowed to reach. As a Tier 2 admin, most of your access tickets begin and end here.

You manage it from two main places: the **Microsoft 365 admin center** for everyday user and licence work, and the **Microsoft Entra admin center** (entra.microsoft.com) for deeper identity controls like Conditional Access.

## Cloud-only vs synced (hybrid) identities

There are two kinds of accounts. A **cloud-only identity** is created and lives entirely in Entra ID. A **synced (hybrid) identity** starts in an on-premises **Active Directory** and is copied up to the cloud by **Microsoft Entra Connect**.

The practical difference matters at the helpdesk: for a synced user, you usually edit the account (name, password, group membership) in on-premises AD, and the change flows up. For a cloud-only user, you edit it directly in the cloud. Always check which type you are dealing with before making changes.

## Users and groups

You create users in the admin center, or with **Microsoft Graph PowerShell**.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "User.ReadWrite.All"
Get-MgUser -UserId "ada@contoso.com"
New-MgUser -DisplayName "Ada Lovelace" -UserPrincipalName "ada@contoso.com" -MailNickname "ada" -AccountEnabled -PasswordProfile @{ Password = "TempP@ssw0rd!"; ForceChangePasswordNextSignIn = $true }
```

Groups come in two flavours you must not confuse. A **security group** controls access to resources and supports licensing. A **Microsoft 365 group** adds shared collaboration: a mailbox, calendar, and Teams/SharePoint space. Use security groups for access and licensing; use Microsoft 365 groups for teams that collaborate.

## Licensing through groups

Assigning licences one user at a time does not scale. Instead use **group-based licensing**: assign the licence to a security group, and every member inherits it automatically.

```text
Microsoft 365 admin center > Billing > Licenses
  -> or Entra admin center > Groups > [group] > Licenses > Assignments
```

When someone joins the group they get the licence; when they leave, it is removed. Joiner and leaver changes become almost automatic.

## MFA and Conditional Access

A password alone is weak. **Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** adds a second factor — typically the **Microsoft Authenticator** app — so a stolen password is not enough.

The modern way to enforce it is **Conditional Access**. A policy reads **signals** (which user, which device, which location, how risky the sign-in) and then makes a **decision**: require MFA, require a compliant device, or block.

```text
Entra admin center > Protection > Conditional Access > Policies > New policy
  Assignments: Users/groups + target apps
  Conditions: locations, device platforms, sign-in risk
  Grant: Require multi-factor authentication
```

Start policies in **report-only** mode so you can see the impact before turning them on.

## Self-service password reset

**Self-service password reset (SSPR)** lets users reset or unlock their own accounts using registered methods like phone or the Authenticator app. Enable it for a group, make users register, and your password-reset ticket volume drops sharply. When SSPR is not available, resets and **account lockouts** are still classic Tier 2 jobs you handle directly in the admin center.

## Your task

In a test or trial tenant, create one cloud-only user, add them to a security group, assign a licence to that group, and build a report-only Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for that group.

hd6-l03-exchange-online-and-email-suppor.title: Exchange Online and email support
objectives: 'Describe Exchange Online and the main mailbox types: user, shared, and resource/room'
Grant shared mailbox access and explain Full Access, Send As, and Send on Behalf
Choose between a distribution group and a Microsoft 365 group for a given need
'Explain mail flow basics: connectors and transport (mail flow) rules'
Run a message trace to answer 'did my email arrive?' tickets and check quarantine
'Triage common email tickets: can''t send/receive, out of office, mailbox full, calendar sharing'
hd6-l03-exchange-online-and-email-suppor.body:
## Exchange Online: cloud email, managed centrally

**Exchange Online** is the hosted email service inside Microsoft 365. Instead of running an on-premises Exchange server, mailboxes live in Microsoft's cloud and you administer them from the **Exchange admin center (EAC)** at `admin.exchange.microsoft.com` or from **Exchange Online PowerShell**. As a Tier 2 tech, this is where most email tickets land, so knowing the moving parts pays off fast.

Connect to PowerShell once and you can do almost anything the portal can, faster:

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline -UserPrincipalName admin@contoso.com
Get-Mailbox -ResultSize 50 | Format-Table DisplayName,RecipientTypeDetails,PrimarySmtpAddress
```

## Mailbox types you will manage

There are three types you meet daily. A **user mailbox** belongs to a licensed person. A **shared mailbox** (think `info@` or `support@`) needs no license under 50 GB and lets several people read and send from one address. A **resource mailbox** represents a **room** or **equipment** you book in Outlook calendars.

```powershell
New-Mailbox -Shared -Name "Support" -PrimarySmtpAddress support@contoso.com
New-Mailbox -Room -Name "Boardroom"
```

## Shared mailbox access and permissions

Three permissions cover almost every shared-mailbox request. **Full Access** lets someone open and read the mailbox. **Send As** makes their messages appear to come purely from the shared address. **Send on Behalf** shows "User on behalf of Mailbox". A common ticket: a user has Full Access but replies still show their own name — they are missing Send As.

```powershell
Add-MailboxPermission -Identity support@contoso.com -User joe@contoso.com -AccessRights FullAccess -AutoMapping $true
Add-RecipientPermission -Identity support@contoso.com -Trustee joe@contoso.com -AccessRights SendAs
```

## Groups: distribution vs Microsoft 365

A **distribution group** simply forwards mail to its members — one address in, many copies out. A **Microsoft 365 group** is a collaboration identity: a shared inbox, calendar, **SharePoint** site and **Teams** all under one membership. Rule of thumb: announcements only -> distribution group; a team that also needs shared files and chat -> Microsoft 365 group.

## Mail flow, message trace, and quarantine

**Mail flow** is how messages move in and out. **Connectors** define routing to or from partner systems, and **mail flow rules** (transport rules) apply conditions and actions — for example, add a disclaimer or block an attachment type. When a user asks "did my email arrive?", run a **message trace**:

```powershell
Get-MessageTrace -SenderAddress joe@contoso.com -StartDate (Get-Date).AddHours(-4) -EndDate (Get-Date)
```

Statuses like **Delivered**, **Pending**, **Failed**, or **Quarantined** tell you the next step. If it is **Quarantined**, check the quarantine in the Microsoft Defender portal and release it if it is a false positive.

```text
Exchange admin center -> Mail flow -> Message trace -> set sender/recipient + time range -> Search
```

## Your task

In a test tenant, create a shared mailbox `helpdesk@yourdomain`, grant a colleague **Full Access** and **Send As**, then send a test message and run a **message trace** to confirm it was Delivered. Note where you would look if the status came back Quarantined instead.

hd6-l04-teams-sharepoint-onedrive-suppor.title: Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive support
objectives: Explain how a Team is backed by a Microsoft 365 group and a SharePoint site, and where Teams files actually
hd6-l04-teams-sharepoint-onedrive-suppor.body:
## How Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive fit together

This is the single most important idea in the lesson: these three services are one connected system. When you create a **Team**, Microsoft 365 quietly provisions a **Microsoft 365 group** behind it. That group brings a **SharePoint site**, a group mailbox, a calendar, and a Planner. Every file someone drops into a Teams channel is actually stored in the **Documents** library of that SharePoint site — Teams is just a friendly front door to SharePoint.

**OneDrive for Business** is the personal version of the same SharePoint storage engine: each user gets their own site for private files. Files shared in a one-to-one or group **chat** (not a channel) live in the sender's OneDrive, not the team site. Knowing where a file physically lives tells you exactly which admin center to open when a ticket lands.

## The Teams admin center

Most Teams tickets are solved with **policies**. Open the Teams admin center to manage them.

```text
admin.teams.microsoft.com
  -> Teams -> Manage teams        (find and own a team)
  -> Meetings -> Meeting policies (recording, lobby, sharing)
  -> Users -> Guest access        (allow/block external guests)
  -> Org-wide settings -> External access
```

**External access** (federation) lets your users chat with people in other Microsoft 365 organisations. **Guest access** lets you add an outside person directly into a team as a guest. They are different switches, and tickets like "I can't add my client to the team" usually trace back to one of them being off.

## SharePoint sites, libraries and sharing

In the SharePoint admin center you manage every site, including the ones created by Teams. The key support concept is **sharing**.

```text
admin.microsoft.com -> SharePoint admin center
  -> Sites -> Active sites        (every site + storage used)
  -> Policies -> Sharing          (tenant external-sharing level)
```

Sharing has two layers. The **tenant** sets the maximum (for example, "Anyone", "New and existing guests", or "Only people in your organisation"), and each **site** can be set equal or more restrictive — never more permissive than the tenant. When someone clicks **Share**, the **link type** matters: a *People in your organisation* link will never work for an external guest. Sharing tickets are almost always a policy level or a wrong link type.

You can also drive this with the SharePoint Online Management Shell:

```powershell
Connect-SPOService -Url https://contoso-admin.sharepoint.com
Get-SPOSite -Limit All | Select Url, Owner, StorageUsageCurrent
Get-SPOSite -Identity https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/Sales | Select SharingCapability
```

## OneDrive and the sync client

The **OneDrive sync client** keeps files mirrored between the PC and the cloud. **Known Folder Move (KFM)** redirects the Desktop, Documents, and Pictures folders into OneDrive so they sync automatically and survive a lost laptop. **Files On-Demand** keeps files cloud-only until opened, saving disk space. When sync stalls, check the blue/grey cloud icons, look for a paused client, an over-quota account, or a filename with illegal characters.

## Common tickets and how you fix them

- **"I lost a file."** Check **version history** first (restore an earlier version), then the **site Recycle Bin** (93 days), then the second-stage Recycle Bin.
- **File sync error.** Reset or restart the sync client, confirm the user is signed in, check storage quota, and rename files with `\ / : * ? " < > |`.
- **Can't access a site or team.** Confirm group membership — access follows the **Microsoft 365 group**, not a one-off permission.
- **Sharing not working.** Check tenant and site external-sharing level, then the link type.
- **Orphaned sites and retention.** Deleting a Team deletes its group and SharePoint site together. A **retention policy** may preserve content even after deletion, and a deleted group can be restored within **30 days**.

## Your task

In a test tenant or lab, create a Team, find its backing SharePoint site in the SharePoint admin center, upload a file to a channel, delete it, and restore it from the site Recycle Bin. Then connect with `Connect-SPOService` and run `Get-SPOSite` to list your sites and their sharing capability.

hd6-l05-m365-security-and-compliance.title: Microsoft 365 security and compliance basics
objectives: Explain the shared-responsibility model and why M365 security and compliance matter
Read Microsoft Secure Score and act on a recommended improvement action
Describe what Microsoft Purview is and the role of a DLP policy
Tell the difference between sensitivity labels and retention labels/policies
Run an audit log search to find who did what, and explain eDiscovery at a high level
Recognise GDPR and other compliance frameworks at an awareness level
hd6-l05-m365-security-and-compliance.body:
## Shared responsibility, and why this matters

Moving to Microsoft 365 does not move security off your plate. Under the **shared-responsibility model**, Microsoft secures the physical datacentres and the underlying platform, but the **customer always owns their data, identities, and access**. That is exactly the layer a helpdesk touches every day — accounts, sharing, and the content users create.

Security and compliance are two sides of the same coin. **Security** keeps attackers and accidents from harming data; **compliance** proves you are handling data according to rules like **GDPR**. As a Tier 2 tech you won't author deep policy, but you must read these tools, report what you find, and take simple corrective actions.

## Microsoft Secure Score

**Microsoft Secure Score** measures your tenant's security posture as a percentage and gives a ranked list of **improvement actions** — for example, enabling multi-factor authentication or blocking legacy authentication. Each action shows the points gained and the user impact.

```text
Microsoft 365 Defender portal (security.microsoft.com)
  > Secure Score
    > Recommended actions  (sort by points / status)
    > pick an action > Manage in integrations
```

Reading it is a skill: look at the highest-value, lowest-impact actions first, and report progress over time.

## Microsoft Purview: the compliance hub

**Microsoft Purview** (at `compliance.microsoft.com` / `purview.microsoft.com`) is where compliance lives — data classification, **data loss prevention**, labels, auditing, and eDiscovery all sit here.

**DLP policies** detect **sensitive information types** (credit-card numbers, passport or national-ID numbers) and can warn a user, block sharing, or restrict access when that data tries to leave.

```text
Microsoft Purview portal
  > Data loss prevention > Policies
    > review policy > Locations (Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams)
    > Rules > conditions (sensitive info types) > actions (block / notify)
```

## Labels: classify, protect, and retain

Two label families do different jobs:

- **Sensitivity labels** *classify and protect* content — they can mark a document **Confidential**, add a watermark, or apply encryption that follows the file.
- **Retention labels** and **retention policies** *control lifecycle* — how long an item is kept and when it is deleted.

```text
Microsoft Purview portal
  > Information protection > Labels        (sensitivity)
  > Data lifecycle management > Retention policies   (retain / delete)
```

## Auditing and eDiscovery

The **audit log** answers "who did what" — sign-ins, file access, external sharing, admin changes. You search it, filter, and report.

```text
Microsoft Purview portal
  > Audit > Search
    > set date range, users, activities > Search > export results
```

You can also check audit status with PowerShell:

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline
Get-AdminAuditLogConfig | Select UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled
```

**eDiscovery** is the process of finding, holding, and exporting content (email, files, chats) for legal cases or investigations. At Tier 2 you should recognise the concept and where it lives in Purview, not run full legal cases.

## Compliance frameworks at a glance

**GDPR** is the headline data-protection framework: it governs how personal data is collected, stored, and handled. Others include **ISO 27001** and **HIPAA**. You don't need to memorise them — just know they drive the labels, DLP, and retention rules you support.

## Your task

Open Secure Score and write down your tenant's current score plus the top three recommended actions. Then in Microsoft Purview, find one DLP policy and note what sensitive information type it protects and what action it takes.

hd6-l06-defender-for-office-365.title: Defender for Office 365 and threat protection
objectives: Explain the difference between Exchange Online Protection (EOP) and Defender for Office 365 Plan 1 and
hd6-l06-defender-for-office-365.body:
## The threat landscape and why layers matter

Most attacks against an organisation arrive by email: **phishing** (tricking a user into giving up credentials), **spoofing** (forging a trusted sender), **malware** (a weaponised attachment or link), and **business email compromise** (a convincing message from a "CEO" asking for a wire transfer). No single filter stops all of these, so Microsoft 365 stacks protection in layers.

The baseline layer is **Exchange Online Protection (EOP)** — every Exchange Online mailbox gets it. EOP handles **anti-spam**, **anti-malware**, **anti-phishing** (spoof intelligence), and **connection filtering**. On top of EOP you can license **Microsoft Defender for Office 365**, sold as **Plan 1** (Safe Attachments, Safe Links, real-time detections) and **Plan 2** (everything in Plan 1 plus automated investigation and response, attack simulation training, and advanced hunting).

## Safe Attachments and Safe Links

**Safe Attachments** opens attachments in an isolated sandbox and watches their behaviour — this is called **detonation**. If the file does something malicious, it never reaches the inbox. **Safe Links** rewrites every URL and re-checks it at the moment the user clicks — **time-of-click** protection. This matters because attackers often send a clean link, then weaponise the destination after delivery, defeating a one-time scan.

```text
Microsoft Defender portal > Email & collaboration > Policies & rules
  > Threat policies > Safe Attachments  (and Safe Links)
```

## Anti-phishing, anti-spam, and anti-malware policies

Policies decide what happens to suspect mail. **Anti-phishing** policies add impersonation and mailbox-intelligence protection; **anti-spam** policies set spam actions and allow/block lists; **anti-malware** policies control the common-attachments filter. You can read them in **Exchange Online PowerShell**.

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline
Get-AntiPhishPolicy | Format-List Name,Enabled,EnableMailboxIntelligence
Get-HostedContentFilterPolicy | Format-List Name,SpamAction,BulkThreshold
```

## Quarantine and end-user release

Messages that policies block land in **quarantine**. As Tier 2 you review them, **release** false positives, and decide whether end users may request release themselves (governed by **quarantine policies**).

```text
Microsoft Defender portal > Email & collaboration
  > Review > Quarantine
```

```powershell
Get-QuarantineMessage -RecipientAddress user@contoso.com
Release-QuarantineMessage -Identity <messageId> -ReleaseToAll
```

When a user emails "why didn't I get this newsletter?", the cleanest fix is to release the message and then allow the sender or tune the policy — never disable protection tenant-wide.

## Threat Explorer, reporting, and the report buttons

**Threat Explorer** (Explorer / Real-time detections) lets you search all mail by sender, subject, URL, or detection verdict, so you can see who else received a campaign. Users help you by clicking the built-in **Report phishing** / **Report message** button in Outlook, which feeds submissions you triage under **Submissions**.

## The Tier-2 triage workflow

When a user reports a suspicious email or admits they clicked a bad link, work a repeatable pattern: **contain**, then **scope**, then **remediate**.

```text
1. Contain: did they enter credentials? Reset password + revoke sessions.
2. Scope: use Threat Explorer to find everyone who got the same message.
3. Check Safe Links click verdicts to confirm what was blocked or allowed.
4. Remediate: purge the message tenant-wide; block sender/URL.
5. Document and escalate to security if the blast radius is wide.
```

## Your task

In the Microsoft Defender portal, open Threat policies and read your tenant's Safe Links, Safe Attachments, and anti-phishing policies. Then connect to Exchange Online PowerShell and run `Get-AntiPhishPolicy` and `Get-QuarantineMessage`, and write a short five-step triage note for a user who clicked a phishing link.

hd6-l07-m365-troubleshooting-and-service.title: Microsoft 365 troubleshooting and service health
objectives: 'Apply a scoping methodology: one user, many users, or a service-wide outage'
Use the Service health dashboard and Message center to rule out a Microsoft-side incident before troubleshooting
hd6-l07-m365-troubleshooting-and-service.body:
## Start by scoping the problem

The biggest time-waster in cloud support is fixing the wrong layer. Before you touch anything, answer one question: **is this one user, many users, or a service outage?** That single decision changes everything you do next.

- **One user** → look at *that* user: licence, mailbox, MFA registration, device, client.
- **Many users / a whole department** → look at *configuration*: a group, a policy, a **Conditional Access** rule, a licence pool.
- **Everyone, suddenly** → suspect a **Microsoft-side incident** before you suspect yourself.

Write the scope down at the top of your ticket. It is the most important line you will record.
