## Rule out Microsoft first: Service health and Message center

If the scope smells like "everyone", check Microsoft's own status before you debug for hours.

```text
Microsoft 365 admin center (admin.microsoft.com)
  > Health > Service health   (active incidents & advisories)
  > Health > Message center   (planned changes & required actions)
```

**Service health** lists incidents Microsoft has acknowledged, the affected services, and an estimated time to resolution. If your symptom matches an active incident, your job switches from *fixing* to *communicating* — post status, link the incident ID, and wait. The **Message center** is different: it announces upcoming changes, new and retiring features, and actions you must take. A change announced there last week often explains "it stopped working" today.

## Confirm where the problem lives: client vs service

When Service health is green, the problem is on your side — but is it the **client** or the **service**? Test from a second device or a browser session. If Outlook on the web works but the desktop client fails, it is a **client** problem. Use the connectivity test and basic checks:

```powershell
# Reachability and DNS sanity from the user's machine
Test-Connection outlook.office365.com -Count 4
Resolve-DnsName outlook.office365.com
```

The **Microsoft 365 connectivity test** (connectivity.office.com) and the admin center's diagnostics run guided checks and surface known issues automatically.

## Check the usual cloud root causes

Most "can't access" tickets come down to a handful of causes. Verify them directly rather than guessing:

```powershell
# Verify the user's licence assignment and account state
Get-MgUser -UserId user@contoso.com -Property AssignedLicenses,AccountEnabled

# Verify mailbox exists and type is correct
Get-Mailbox user@contoso.com | Format-List Name,RecipientTypeDetails,LitigationHoldEnabled
```

The big three: a **missing or wrong licence**, an **MFA** registration problem, and a **Conditional Access** policy blocking the sign-in (check the Entra sign-in logs for the failure reason). These explain far more outages than broken software does.

## Use SARA for client-side Office issues

For Outlook, Office activation, and Microsoft 365 sign-in problems on a device, download and run the **Support and Recovery Assistant (SARA)**. It runs automated diagnostics, fixes many issues on the spot, and when it cannot, it collects logs you can attach to a support case — saving a round-trip with Microsoft.

## Escalate cleanly when it is genuinely Microsoft's

If you have confirmed it is a service issue and there is no published incident, open a support request from **Help & support** in the admin center. Include: impact, **scope** (who and how many), exact error text, **timestamps with time zone**, the affected service and region, what you have already tried, and diagnostic or connectivity-test output. Document the same in your ticket so the next tech is not starting from zero.

## Your task

Take a real or sample ticket and write out its troubleshooting trail: state the scope (one user / many / outage), record the Service health result, note client-vs-service, list the three root-cause checks you ran, and draft the support-request summary you would send Microsoft.

hd6-l08-ai-in-m365-copilot.title: AI in Microsoft 365: Copilot adoption and support
objectives: Explain what Microsoft 365 Copilot is and how it grounds responses in your organisation's data via Microsoft
hd6-l08-ai-in-m365-copilot.body:
## What Microsoft 365 Copilot actually is

**Microsoft 365 Copilot** is a large language model (an **LLM**) woven into the apps your users already live in — Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams. The thing that makes it useful at work is **grounding**: instead of answering from generic training data alone, Copilot pulls in your organisation's own content — emails, documents, chats, and calendar — through **Microsoft Graph**. Ask it to "summarise last week's project emails and draft a status update" and it reads the real threads the user can already see, then writes the draft.

The key Tier 2 mental model: Copilot is the model, **Microsoft Graph** is how it finds your data, and the user's **Entra ID** identity is what scopes what it may touch.

## Prerequisites before anyone can use it

Three things must line up. First, an eligible **Microsoft 365 Copilot licence** (a paid add-on) assigned to the user. Second, **supported app versions** — Copilot lives in current builds of the Microsoft 365 apps, so an out-of-date client simply will not show it. Third, a cloud **Entra ID** account, because Copilot uses that identity to decide what data it can reach.

## Permissions, and why oversharing is now a risk

This is the point examiners and security teams care about most. **Copilot never shows a user data they could not already access.** It honours the exact same permissions the user already has — it does not elevate anything.

The catch: many tenants have quietly **overshared** in SharePoint for years — "Everyone" links, wide site access, forgotten permissions. Before Copilot, that content was hard to stumble across. After Copilot, a single prompt like "what's our pricing strategy?" can surface it instantly. Copilot did not break permissions; it just made loose permissions visible. **Clean up oversharing before rollout.**

## The data protection boundary

Under **commercial data protection**, your prompts, the data Copilot retrieves through Graph, and the responses it generates are **not used to train the underlying foundation models**, and stay inside your Microsoft 365 service boundary. Copilot inherits your existing compliance controls — sensitivity labels, retention, and audit. Be ready to reassure nervous users and managers on this.

## Assigning Copilot licences

Licences are assigned per user in the **Microsoft 365 admin center**:

```text
Microsoft 365 admin center (admin.microsoft.com)
  > Users > Active users
  > select the user > Licenses and apps
  > tick "Microsoft 365 Copilot" > Save changes
```

For bulk assignment, group-based licensing or PowerShell scales better:

```powershell
# Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "User.ReadWrite.All","Directory.ReadWrite.All"
# inspect a user's current licences
Get-MgUserLicenseDetail -UserId "jordan@contoso.com" | Select SkuPartNumber
```

## Common tickets and adoption support

"**Copilot isn't showing up**" — almost always no licence assigned, or an old app build; check both. **Expectation management** — users expect magic and get a helpful-but-imperfect assistant. **Hallucinations** — Copilot can sound confident and still be wrong, so coach users to treat every output as a draft and verify against the source. **Adoption** — better prompts get better results: give it a goal, context, and a desired format ("Draft a 3-bullet summary of this thread for my manager").

The Tier 2 role in a rollout: confirm prerequisites, assign and track licences, help remediate oversharing with the security team, and field the first wave of support tickets.

## Your task

In a test tenant, assign a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence to one user via the admin center, confirm Copilot appears in their Word and Teams, then write a one-page support note explaining the "Copilot isn't showing up" checklist and how to coach users on verifying outputs.

hd6-l09-tier2-capstone.title: Tier 2 capstone: end-to-end incident handling
objectives: Triage a user report and rule out a service outage before assuming compromise
Investigate suspicious sign-ins in Microsoft Entra ID and confirm scope
Contain a compromised account by resetting credentials and revoking active sessions
Find and remove attacker persistence such as inbox rules and mail forwarding
Use message trace, quarantine, and Defender to assess spread and remediate
Communicate, escalate, and write clear root-cause and post-incident notes in the ticket
hd6-l09-tier2-capstone.body:
## The ticket lands

A user, Priya, raises a ticket: she **can't send email**, and two colleagues have asked her why she emailed them a strange "shared invoice" link. This is your capstone. Everything you learned this course — hardware and OS basics, networking, identity, email, security, and Microsoft 365 admin — comes together in one incident. You will work it end to end like a real **Tier 2** tech.

Don't jump to a fix. Start with **triage**: when did it start, what exactly does "can't send" look like (a bounce? a block?), and has anything changed. Log it in the ticket as you go.

## Rule out an outage first

Before you assume compromise, confirm scope. Open the Microsoft 365 admin center and check **Service health**.

```text
Microsoft 365 admin center > Health > Service health > Exchange Online
```

If there's an active advisory affecting send/receive, this may be a platform incident, not Priya. No advisory, and only Priya is affected with odd outbound mail? That points at an **account compromise** — likely the aftermath of a phishing link that harvested her password.

## Investigate the sign-ins

Go to **Microsoft Entra ID** and review Priya's sign-in logs. You're looking for **impossible travel**, sign-ins from an unfamiliar country, and **legacy authentication** attempts.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "AuditLog.Read.All","User.ReadWrite.All"
Get-MgAuditLogSignIn -Filter "userPrincipalName eq 'priya@contoso.com'" -Top 25 |
  Select-Object createdDateTime, ipAddress, @{n='City';e={$_.Location.City}}, status
```

A successful sign-in from another continent minutes after a normal one confirms it. Note the timeline in the ticket.

## Contain the account

Now stop the bleeding, in order. **Reset the password**, then **revoke active sessions** so any tokens the attacker already holds stop working, then re-confirm **MFA**.

```powershell
# Disable sign-in while you work, then revoke live tokens
Update-MgUser -UserId priya@contoso.com -AccountEnabled:$false
Revoke-MgUserSignInSession -UserId priya@contoso.com
```

Reset the password in the admin center, re-enable the account, and confirm MFA is registered. The stolen credential is now useless.

## Remove persistence and assess spread

A password reset alone is not enough. Attackers plant **inbox rules** and **mail forwarding** to keep reading mail and hide replies. Connect to Exchange Online and check.

```powershell
Connect-ExchangeOnline
Get-InboxRule -Mailbox priya@contoso.com | Format-List Name, Description, ForwardTo, DeleteMessage
Get-Mailbox priya@contoso.com | Format-List ForwardingSmtpAddress
```

Delete any rule you didn't expect. Then run a **message trace** to see what actually went out and to whom, and check **quarantine** and **Microsoft Defender for Office 365** for the phishing message and its blast radius.

```powershell
Get-MessageTrace -SenderAddress priya@contoso.com -StartDate (Get-Date).AddDays(-2) -EndDate (Get-Date)
```

## Communicate, escalate, document

Tell Priya what happened in plain language and that her account is secure. Warn the colleagues who received the link **not to click it**. If the spread is wide or other accounts look affected, **escalate** to Tier 3 / security. Finally, write the **root-cause and post-incident note** in the ticket: timeline, likely cause (phishing), actions taken, and follow-ups such as security-awareness training and tighter conditional access.

## Your task

Write the full incident up as a single ticket: triage notes, the outage check, the sign-in evidence, your containment steps, the persistence you removed, the message-trace findings, and a three-line root-cause note. Treat it as the write-up you'd hand to a hiring manager.

hd6-l10-certification-roadmap-and-job-se.title: Certification roadmap and job-search playbook
objectives: Order the core certifications and explain which goal each one serves
Choose your next certification based on the role you want
Write quantified, tailored resume bullets that map to a job description
Build a portfolio from your home lab and the projects in this course
Answer behavioral questions with the STAR method
Talk confidently about your troubleshooting methodology in an interview
hd6-l10-certification-roadmap-and-job-se.body:
## The certification ladder, and why order matters

Certifications are not a checklist — they are a **ladder** that signals a story to employers. Each rung proves a capability the next role expects. The trick is to climb in an order that matches the job you actually want, not to collect badges for their own sake.

Here is the ladder this course points you toward:

```text
  AI-900  (AI literacy differentiator — bolt on anytime)
     ^
  MS-102  (Microsoft 365 Administrator)  <-- your current target
     ^
  MD-102  (Endpoint / device admin with Intune)
     ^
  Network+  (networking foundations)
     ^
  A+  (hardware, OS, core troubleshooting — the base)
```

## Which cert to chase, and when

**CompTIA A+** is the foundation. If you are brand new, start here: hardware, operating systems, and the troubleshooting mindset every helpdesk role assumes. **CompTIA Network+** is the natural second step — DNS, DHCP, subnets, and the network knowledge that turns "it's broken" into "it's a DNS issue."

From there you specialise. **Microsoft MD-102 (Endpoint Administrator)** validates deploying and securing Windows devices with **Intune** — ideal if you want a device-management or modern-desktop role. **Microsoft MS-102 (Microsoft 365 Administrator)** is your current target: tenant identity, licensing, Exchange Online, and security and compliance. It maps directly to the Tier 2 / M365 admin work you have practiced all month.

**Microsoft AI-900 (Azure AI Fundamentals)** is the differentiator. It is a fundamentals exam, not a deep specialism, but on a 2026 resume it signals **AI literacy** — and it is a quick win you can bolt on at any point.

## Resume and CV: prove it, don't claim it

A resume that says "good at troubleshooting" is invisible. A resume that **quantifies** is hired. Tailor every application to the **job description (JD)**: mirror its keywords so you pass the **applicant-tracking system (ATS)**, and list your certifications near the top.

Use this bullet template:

```text
[Action verb] + [what you did] + [tool/tech] + [measurable result]

Examples:
- Resolved 40+ Tier 1 tickets per week in Microsoft 365,
  maintaining a 96% first-contact-resolution rate.
- Migrated 120 mailboxes to Exchange Online with zero data loss.
- Cut onboarding time 30% by automating user setup in Intune.
```

## Build a portfolio that backs it up

Certs say you can pass an exam; a **portfolio** shows you can do the work. Build a **home lab** — a free Microsoft 365 developer tenant, a couple of test users, an Intune policy or two. Document each project: the problem, your steps, screenshots, the result. The labs and tickets from this course are portfolio pieces already — write them up. A simple repo or one-page site that says "here is what I built and how" beats a wall of buzzwords.

## Interview prep: methodology over memorisation

Expect two flavours of question. **Behavioral** questions ("Tell me about a time a user was frustrated") want a story — answer with **STAR**: Situation, Task, Action, Result, ending on a measurable outcome. **Technical** questions ("A user can't reach a network share — walk me through it") want your **troubleshooting methodology**: gather information, establish a theory, test it, fix, verify, document. They care less about the single right answer and more about how you *think*.

Practice saying out loud: "First I'd reproduce it, then check what changed, then isolate the layer — user, device, network, or service." That sentence wins interviews.

## Your task

Three steps. First, **pick your next certification** and write one sentence on why it fits your target role. Second, **draft three quantified resume bullets** using the template above, drawn from real work or your course labs. Third, **outline a portfolio** — list three projects you could document this month, each with a one-line problem statement.

ht1-l01-the-tier3-mindset-and-rca.title: The Tier 3 mindset: escalation engineering and RCA
objectives: Distinguish a symptom, a proximate cause, and a true root cause on a real incident
Apply the difference between mitigation, remediation, and root-cause elimination
Build a falsifiable hypothesis and design the cheapest test that disproves it
Capture defensible evidence with timestamps, hashes, and a reproducible method
Decide when to stop investigating and accept a documented unknown
Scope an escalation so Tier 1 and Tier 2 know exactly what was ruled out
ht1-l01-the-tier3-mindset-and-rca.body:
## From ticket-closer to root-cause engineer

At Tier 1 and Tier 2 your job was speed: restore the user, close the ticket, move on. At **Tier 3** the unit of work changes. You are no longer paid to make a symptom disappear — you are paid to find why it happened and make sure it never happens to the rest of the fleet. That shift demands a different discipline: evidence over instinct, hypotheses over hunches, and elimination over guessing.

The core trap to avoid is treating a **mitigation** as a fix. Restarting a hung service, clearing a cache, or reimaging a machine restores service — but if you cannot say *why* it broke, you have only bought time. The fault is still latent in every other machine.

## Symptom, proximate cause, root cause

Every incident has three layers. The **symptom** is what the user reports ("VPN drops"). The **proximate cause** is the immediate technical trigger ("the VPN service faults when the adapter renegotiates"). The **root cause** is the underlying condition that allowed the trigger to exist and recur ("a driver pushed without version pinning regresses the adapter").

Tier 2 fixes proximate causes. Tier 3 eliminates root causes. If your fix only changes the proximate layer, expect the ticket to reopen across the fleet.

## Hypotheses you can disprove

Good investigation is an **elimination game**, not a confirmation hunt. State each theory as a **falsifiable hypothesis** — a claim a specific test could prove wrong. Then run the *cheapest test that kills the most hypotheses first*. Resist the urge to run the test that confirms your favourite theory; confirmation bias is the single biggest time-sink in RCA.

Start by establishing a baseline with Reliability Monitor and event timelines:

```powershell
# Pull the recent reliability/stability events into a timeline
Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 200 |
  Where-Object { $_.LevelDisplayName -in 'Error','Critical' } |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, Message |
  Sort-Object TimeCreated
```

## Evidence that survives challenge

Tier 3 findings get questioned — by vendors, by management, by the next engineer. Make your work **defensible**. Capture exact timestamps so you can correlate across logs, dumps, and traces. Hash any artefact you rely on so nobody can claim it was altered.

```powershell
# Hash a captured dump or log so the evidence is tamper-evident
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 'C:\evidence\MEMORY.DMP'

# Record a precise, sortable timestamp for your notes
Get-Date -Format 'o'
```

A defensible RCA is one another engineer can reproduce from your notes alone. If they cannot rebuild your reasoning, you have a story, not a root cause.

## Knowing when to stop

Not every cause can be proven with the evidence available. The mark of maturity is a **bounded unknown**: you document every hypothesis tested, what ruled it out, the monitored mitigation you applied, and exactly what new data would let you resume. That is honest engineering. An abandoned ticket dressed up as "intermittent" is not.

## Your task

Take a real recurring incident from your queue (or a deliberately broken test VM). Write a one-page RCA scope: list the symptom, your candidate proximate causes, and at least three falsifiable hypotheses for the root cause. For each hypothesis, name the single cheapest test that would disprove it, and rank them so the first test eliminates the most theories. Collect a System event timeline with `Get-WinEvent`, hash one artefact, and record ISO-8601 timestamps. Conclude with either a proven root cause or an explicitly bounded unknown.

ht1-l02-advanced-windows-internals.title: Advanced Windows internals: boot, registry, services & drivers
objectives: Trace the Windows boot sequence from firmware through Session Manager to the desktop
Explain how the registry HKLM\SYSTEM control sets and LastKnownGood are selected
Read a driver's Start type and ErrorControl and predict its effect on boot
Map service dependency chains and diagnose a failed dependency
Use Autoruns and the boot/setup event logs to find what runs at startup
Distinguish a kernel-mode driver fault from a user-mode service failure
ht1-l02-advanced-windows-internals.body:
## The boot sequence, end to end

To diagnose a machine that never reaches the desktop, you must know the order things happen. **Firmware** (UEFI) hands off to the **Windows Boot Manager** (`bootmgr`), which reads the **BCD** store and starts the **Windows OS Loader** (`winload.efi`). The loader pulls in the kernel (`ntoskrnl.exe`), the HAL, and every **Boot-start driver**. The kernel initialises, then starts **Session Manager** (`smss.exe`) — the first user-mode process. Smss sets up the registry, paging files, and environment, runs autochk, then launches the session leading to **Winlogon** and the desktop.

If a machine hangs on the spinner, the fault is usually before smss (a Boot/System driver). If it reaches the logon screen and then fails, you are in user-mode service territory.

## Control sets and LastKnownGood

The live system configuration lives under `HKLM\SYSTEM`. Windows keeps multiple numbered **control sets** and records which is which under `HKLM\SYSTEM\Select`.

```text
HKLM\SYSTEM\Select\Current        -> e.g. 1  (the ControlSet booted now)
HKLM\SYSTEM\Select\LastKnownGood  -> e.g. 1  (last config that reached logon)
HKLM\SYSTEM\Select\Failed         -> e.g. 2
```

**LastKnownGood** is updated to the current set only after a *successful* interactive logon. That is why "Last Known Good Configuration" can recover a machine that a bad driver just broke — it rolls back to the set that last reached the desktop.

## Drivers: Start type and ErrorControl

Every driver and service has a **Start** type and an **ErrorControl** value under its `Services` key:

```powershell
# Inspect a driver's load behaviour
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\disk' |
  Select-Object Start, Type, ErrorControl, ImagePath
```

**Start**: 0 = Boot, 1 = System, 2 = Auto, 3 = Demand, 4 = Disabled. **ErrorControl**: 0 = Ignore, 1 = Normal, 2 = Severe, 3 = Critical. A Boot-start driver (0) with Critical error control (3) that fails will bugcheck or force a LastKnownGood rollback. A Demand-start driver (3) that fails usually only breaks the feature that needed it. Reading these two numbers tells you whether a fault is a no-boot or a nuisance.

## Services and dependency chains

Services start in dependency order under the **Service Control Manager** (SCM). If service A lists B in `DependOnService` and B fails, SCM refuses to start A.

```powershell
# Dump a service's full config including its dependencies
sc.exe qc Netlogon

# List what depends on a given service
Get-Service -Name LanmanWorkstation -DependentServices
```

A single failed low-level service can cascade into a dozen downstream failures — always trace upstream to the first thing that broke, not the loudest error.

## Auditing what actually runs

**Autoruns** from Sysinternals enumerates every autostart location: drivers, services, Run keys, scheduled tasks, codecs, and more, with signature verification. Use it to spot an unsigned or unexpected driver loading early. Pair it with the boot performance and setup logs:

```powershell
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Diagnostics-Performance/Operational' |
  Where-Object Id -in 100,101,102,103 |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message -First 20
```

## Your task

On a test VM, read `HKLM\SYSTEM\Select` and record which control set is Current and which is LastKnownGood. Pick three drivers and use `Get-ItemProperty` to list their Start and ErrorControl values; for each, predict in writing what would happen on boot if it failed to load. Run Autoruns, export the list, and identify any unsigned autostart entry. Finally, pick a multi-dependency service (e.g. Netlogon), map its dependency chain with `sc.exe qc` and `Get-Service -DependentServices`, and draw the chain.

ht1-l03-performance-analysis.title: Performance analysis and bottleneck hunting
objectives: Decompose 'slow' into a measurable bottleneck across CPU, memory, disk, and GPU
Use Performance Monitor counters to distinguish saturation from latency
Identify hard page faults and committed-memory pressure versus working-set churn
Capture a CPU and disk profile with Windows Performance Recorder (WPR)
Open and read the trace in Windows Performance Analyzer (WPA) to find the hot stack
Tell a genuine resource bottleneck apart from a scheduling or contention problem
ht1-l03-performance-analysis.body:
## 'Slow' is not a measurement

The word **slow** is a symptom, never a cause. Your first job is to turn it into a number: which resource is constrained, and is the problem **saturation** (the resource is maxed out) or **latency** (the resource is idle but answering slowly)? These have opposite fixes, and utilisation percentages alone cannot tell them apart. A disk at 5% busy that takes 40 ms per IO will make a machine feel terrible while every dashboard looks green.

## The four-resource sweep, plus the ones people miss

Start with the obvious four — **CPU, memory, disk, network** — but go beyond utilisation. For each, ask both *how busy* and *how slow per operation*.

```text
CPU     : % usage, but also queue length and DPC/interrupt time
Memory  : Available MB, AND hard page-fault rate (paging to disk)
Disk    : % busy, AND avg sec/transfer (latency per IO)
Network : throughput, AND round-trip latency and retransmits
```

Then check the ones people forget: **GPU** (compositor and rendering waits), **handle/thread leaks**, and **lock contention**. A process climbing in handles or threads over hours is a leak you will only see by trending.

## Counters that reveal the truth

Performance Monitor exposes the diagnostic counters Task Manager hides.

```powershell
# Sample the high-value counters once a second for 30 seconds
Get-Counter -Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time',
  '\Memory\Available MBytes',
  '\Memory\Pages/sec',
  '\PhysicalDisk(_Total)\Avg. Disk sec/Transfer',
  '\System\Processor Queue Length' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 30
```

Memory pressure shows up as **hard page faults** (`Pages/sec` driven by reads from disk), not as low Available MB alone. A persistently non-zero `Processor Queue Length` means threads are waiting for a core — contention, not raw CPU shortage.

## Capturing a real profile with WPR

Utilisation tells you *something* is busy; a trace tells you *what* and *why*. **Windows Performance Recorder (WPR)** drives **Event Tracing for Windows (ETW)** to capture sampled CPU stacks, context switches, and disk IO over time.

```powershell
# Start a CPU + disk profile, reproduce the slowness, then stop
wpr -start CPU -start DiskIO
# ... reproduce the slow operation now ...
wpr -stop C:\evidence\slow.etl
```

## Reading it in WPA

Open the `.etl` in **Windows Performance Analyzer (WPA)**. In the CPU Usage (Sampled) graph, expand by process then by stack to find the **hot stack** — the call path consuming the most samples. Crucially, read the thread states: time in **Running** is real CPU work; time in **Ready** means the thread was runnable but starved of a core (contention); time in **Waiting** points at IO or a lock. A thread mostly in Ready is a scheduling problem, not a CPU-capacity problem — a completely different fix.

## Your task

Reproduce a slow scenario on a test machine (or run a CPU/IO-heavy workload). Capture 30 seconds of the PerfMon counters above with `Get-Counter` and decide whether you are seeing saturation or latency. Then capture a WPR trace covering the slow operation, open it in WPA, and identify the hot stack and the dominant thread state (Running, Ready, or Waiting). Write a two-paragraph finding: name the constrained resource, classify it as saturation vs latency vs contention, and state the responsible module from the stack.

ht1-l04-crash-and-hang-analysis.title: Crash and hang analysis: BSODs, dumps & WinDbg basics
objectives: Configure Windows to capture the right dump type for kernel and user crashes
Resolve symbols correctly so WinDbg can name modules and functions
Run !analyze -v and interpret the bugcheck code and faulting module
Distinguish a hang from a crash and capture a manual dump of a frozen process
Read a basic call stack to attribute a fault to a specific driver or DLL
Decide when a crash is a driver defect versus corrupted state versus hardware
ht1-l04-crash-and-hang-analysis.body:
## A crash is data, not a mystery

A blue screen — a **bugcheck** — is the kernel deliberately stopping because continuing would corrupt the system. That stop produces a **crash dump**: a snapshot of memory you can read after the fact. A frozen app produces no dump on its own, but you can force one. Either way, the crash is not a mystery; it is evidence waiting for a debugger.

## Capture the right dump

Before you can analyse, you must capture. For kernel crashes the **Kernel memory dump** (or the modern **Automatic** setting) is the right default: it holds enough kernel memory to name the faulting driver and read the stack, without the disk cost of a **Complete** dump.

```powershell
# Confirm the configured dump type (CrashDumpEnabled: 1=Complete,2=Kernel,7=Automatic)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CrashControl' |
  Select-Object CrashDumpEnabled, DumpFile, AutoReboot
```

Kernel dumps land at `%SystemRoot%\MEMORY.DMP`. Minidumps go to `%SystemRoot%\Minidump`.

## Symbols first, always

WinDbg maps raw addresses to function names using **symbols**. Without them every frame is a hex address and the analysis is useless. Point WinDbg at the Microsoft public symbol server before anything else.

```text
.sympath srv*C:\symbols*https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols
.reload /f
```

If you ever see *"symbols could not be loaded"*, fix the symbol path and `.reload` — do not interpret a stack until names resolve.

## !analyze -v: the first real command

The workhorse is `!analyze -v` ("analyze, dash v" for verbose). It decodes the **bugcheck code**, identifies the likely **faulting module**, and prints the stack at the point of failure.

```text
!analyze -v

*** look for these lines ***
BUGCHECK_CODE:  D1            (DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL)
MODULE_NAME:    somedriver
IMAGE_NAME:     somedriver.sys
FAILURE_BUCKET_ID: ...
```

The bugcheck code classifies *what rule was broken*. `MODULE_NAME`/`IMAGE_NAME` name the code executing at the fault — your prime proximate suspect. But stay disciplined: a faulting module can be the *victim* of corruption another driver caused upstream. Read the full stack with `k`, and check for recently loaded or unsigned drivers with `lm` before assigning root cause.

## Hangs: capture the frozen state

A hang never bugchecks, so you capture the live process. Use **ProcDump** or Task Manager's *Create dump file*.

```text
procdump -ma <pid-or-name> C:\evidence\hang.dmp
```

Open the user-mode dump, run `!analyze -v -hang`, and inspect threads with `~*k` to see what each is waiting on — a lock, a remote call, or a deadlock between two threads. Look for a thread blocked inside a critical section while another thread owns it: that ownership cycle is the signature of a classic deadlock, and the call stacks usually name the component responsible.

## Your task

On a test VM, confirm the configured dump type via the `CrashControl` registry key and set it to Automatic if it is not. Trigger or obtain a kernel dump (a test crash, or an existing MEMORY.DMP), open it in WinDbg, set the symbol path to the public server, and run `!analyze -v`. Record the bugcheck code, the named module, and the top of the stack from `k`. Then capture a user-mode dump of a deliberately hung process with ProcDump, run `~*k`, and write one sentence on what the main thread was waiting on. Conclude with whether your evidence points to a driver defect, corrupted state, or hardware.

ht1-l05-advanced-network-diagnostics.title: Advanced network diagnostics with Wireshark
objectives: Capture traffic at the right point and with the right scope using netsh trace and Wireshark
Write precise display filters to isolate a single conversation
Read the TCP three-way handshake and identify where a connection fails
Use TCP analysis flags to distinguish packet loss from latency from app stalls
Measure round-trip time and time-to-first-byte from a capture
Decide from evidence whether the fault is client, network path, or server
ht1-l05-advanced-network-diagnostics.body:
## Packets do not lie

When a network complaint reaches Tier 3, the argument is usually "it's the network" versus "it's the app." A **packet capture** settles it with evidence. The skill is not capturing — it is reading: knowing which handful of packets answer the question, and filtering out the thousands that do not.

## Capture at the right point and scope

Where you capture decides what you can conclude. A capture on only the affected client cannot distinguish *never sent* from *lost in transit*. Capture at both ends (or use a tap/SPAN port) so you can compare. On Windows you can capture without installing anything using **netsh trace**, then convert the `.etl` for Wireshark, or capture directly in Wireshark.

```powershell
# Lightweight built-in capture; reproduce the issue, then stop
netsh trace start capture=yes tracefile=C:\evidence\net.etl maxsize=512
# ... reproduce the problem ...
netsh trace stop
```

Keep captures short and scoped — a 30-second capture of one reproduction beats an hour of noise.

## Filter down to one conversation

Wireshark's power is its **display filters**. Start broad, then narrow to the single conversation that matters.

```text
ip.addr == 10.20.5.10 && tcp.port == 443
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0      # just the SYNs (connection starts)
dns                                            # name resolution timing
tcp.analysis.flags                             # all the TCP problem indicators
```

Right-click a packet and choose **Follow > TCP Stream** to see one conversation end to end.

## Read the handshake, then the timing

Every TCP connection opens with a three-way handshake: **SYN**, **SYN-ACK**, **ACK**. If the SYN goes unanswered, the connection never forms — a firewall or a dead server. If the handshake completes fast but the first data byte is slow, the network is fine and the **server think-time** (time-to-first-byte) is the problem. This single distinction resolves most "slow app" tickets.

## TCP analysis flags: loss vs latency vs stall

Wireshark's expert analysis labels the symptoms for you:

```text
TCP Retransmission / Fast Retransmission  -> packet loss on the path
TCP Dup ACK (repeated)                    -> receiver signalling a gap (loss)
TCP Zero Window                           -> receiver's buffer full (slow app)
TCP Out-Of-Order                          -> path reordering / multipath
```

Loss (retransmissions and dup ACKs) points at the **network path**. A **Zero Window** is flow control — the *receiving application* is not reading fast enough, so it is an app problem, not a network one. Latency with no loss and a clean window points at distance or a slow hop. **Out-of-order** segments suggest path reordering or load-balanced multipath, which can also trigger spurious retransmissions. Each pattern routes the ticket to a different owner, so name the pattern before you name a team.

## Your task

Reproduce a real or simulated slow/failing network operation. Capture it with `netsh trace` (or directly in Wireshark) for under a minute. In Wireshark, filter to the single conversation with an `ip.addr`/`tcp.port` filter, then Follow the TCP Stream. Measure: handshake time, time-to-first-byte, and any `tcp.analysis.flags` hits. Decide and write down whether the evidence shows packet loss (network path), a Zero Window (receiving app), DNS delay, or server think-time — and state which team you would route it to and why.

ht1-l06-log-analysis-at-scale.title: Log analysis at scale
objectives: Query Windows event logs precisely with Get-WinEvent and FilterHashtable
Build a cross-source timeline by correlating events on time and identifier
Recognise the difference between a noisy symptom log and the originating event
Aggregate events across many machines to separate a one-off from a fleet pattern
Write KQL queries to summarise, bin by time, and rank failures
Avoid the survivorship and selection biases that distort log-based conclusions
ht1-l06-log-analysis-at-scale.body:
## One machine is an anecdote; the fleet is the evidence

At Tier 2 you read one machine's Event Viewer. At Tier 3 the question changes: *is this a one-off, or a pattern across the fleet?* A crash on one laptop is an anecdote. The same crash on forty laptops after the same patch is a root cause. Scaling your log analysis from one host to many is the core Tier 3 skill in this lesson.

## Filter precisely, and server-side

The most common performance mistake is filtering in PowerShell instead of in the log engine. Piping `Get-WinEvent` to `Where-Object` reads and deserialises *every* record first. **FilterHashtable** pushes the filter down into the logging subsystem, so only matching records are ever materialised — often orders of magnitude faster on a busy log.

```powershell
# Precise, fast, server-side filtering
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName   = 'System'
  Id        = 7000,7001,7031,7034   # service control manager failures
  StartTime = (Get-Date).AddHours(-24)
} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, Message
```

## Find the originating event, not the loudest one

Logs are full of **symptom records**. When a low-level service dies, dozens of components log that they lost a dependency. The loudest, most frequent error is usually a *downstream symptom*. RCA means tracing back to the **first, quieter originating event** on the timeline.

Build a cross-source timeline by merging logs and sorting on time:

```powershell
$logs = foreach ($l in 'System','Application') {
  Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = $l; StartTime = (Get-Date).AddHours(-2) }
}
$logs | Sort-Object TimeCreated | Select-Object TimeCreated, LogName, Id, ProviderName
```

The event at the *top* of the cascade — the first failure — is your suspect.

## Aggregate across the fleet with KQL

When logs are centralised (e.g. in a log analytics workspace), **Kusto Query Language (KQL)** lets you separate a one-off from a fleet-wide pattern. The key move is to summarise and bin by time.

```text
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventID in (7031, 7034)
| summarize count() by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| sort by count_ desc
```

Binning turns raw events into a **rate over time**, so a spike at a deployment window jumps out. Summarising by `Computer` tells you whether one host or forty are affected — the difference between an anecdote and a root cause.

## Beware the biases

Two biases wreck log-based RCA. **Selection/survivorship bias**: investigating only escalated tickets samples a skewed subset, making a common problem look rare. **Confirmation bias**: filtering for the events you already expect and never querying the rest. Always query the *whole population* and let the data tell you the prevalence.

## Your task

Using a real or lab fleet (or several machines), write a `FilterHashtable` query that pulls service-control failures (IDs 7000/7001/7031/7034) from the last 24 hours and confirm it runs faster than the `Where-Object` equivalent. Merge System and Application logs into one sorted timeline and identify the first originating event behind a cascade. If you have a log analytics workspace, write a KQL query that `summarize`s those failures by `Computer` and `bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)`; if not, replicate the aggregation in PowerShell with `Group-Object`. Write one paragraph stating whether the issue is a one-off or a fleet pattern, and which bias you actively guarded against.

ht1-l07-rca-frameworks.title: Systematic RCA frameworks
objectives: Apply Five Whys without stopping at the first convenient cause
Use a fault tree to enumerate and eliminate contributing conditions
Run a differential diagnosis to rank competing hypotheses by evidence
Apply the contributing-factors model to incidents with multiple causes
Choose the right framework for the shape of the problem in front of you
Recognise and counter the cognitive biases that derail systematic RCA
ht1-l07-rca-frameworks.body:
## Frameworks beat hunches

The difference between a senior engineer and a lucky one is **repeatability**. A framework forces you to enumerate hypotheses, test the right one next, and recognise when you have actually reached a cause rather than a convenient stopping point. No single method fits every problem — your skill is matching the framework to the *shape* of the incident.

## Five Whys: follow the chain, don't stop at the person

**Five Whys** repeatedly asks "why?" to walk from symptom to cause. It suits problems with a fairly **linear cause chain**. The classic failure is stopping at *human error* — "the tech forgot the config." That is a symptom of a systemic gap, not a root cause. Keep going:

```text
Symptom : VPN config missing on 30 machines
Why 1   : The deploy script skipped them        -> why?
Why 2   : They were offline at deploy time       -> why?
Why 3   : No retry for offline machines          -> why?
Why 4   : The tool has no state tracking         -> why?
Why 5   : No validation that config = intended   <- systemic root cause
```

The useful root cause is the **systemic gap** that let the error happen *and* go undetected — not the person.

## Fault trees: when causes combine

When several conditions can each contribute, a linear chain is the wrong model. A **fault tree** decomposes the top-level failure into contributing conditions joined by **AND/OR** logic, so you can enumerate and *eliminate* combinations rather than chase one thread.

```text
            [App fails to launch]
                   OR
      +-------------+-------------+
  [DLL missing]            [License check fails]
                                AND
                       +----------+----------+
                 [No network]        [Cache expired]
```

You then rule out branches with evidence until only a supported path remains. Fault trees shine for intermittent issues with multiple necessary conditions.

## Differential diagnosis: rank, then discriminate

Borrowed from medicine, **differential diagnosis** lists every plausible cause, ranks them by current evidence, and then chooses the test whose result best **discriminates** between the top contenders — maximising information per test. After each test you re-rank. This is the disciplined version of the "cheapest test that kills the most hypotheses" instinct from Lesson 1.

## Contributing factors: incidents rarely have one cause

Many real incidents have **no single root cause**. The **Swiss-cheese model** says several latent weaknesses had to align: a bad config *and* a missing monitor *and* a slow response. The **contributing-factors** approach captures all of them, so your fixes land at multiple layers rather than scapegoating one. If you only ever find one cause, you are probably stopping too early.

## Countering the biases

Every framework exists partly to defeat **cognitive bias**. **Confirmation bias** makes you over-weight evidence for your favourite theory; counter it by stating, up front, *what evidence would disprove* your leading hypothesis and then actively seeking it. **Anchoring** locks you to the first explanation you heard; **recency bias** makes the last incident feel like this one. Naming the bias is the first step to neutralising it.

## Your task

Take one of your investigations from Lessons 3-6. First, run a written Five Whys and deliberately push past any "human error" stopping point to a systemic gap. Then re-model the same incident as a fault tree with at least one AND and one OR node, and mark which branches your evidence eliminated. List your hypotheses as a ranked differential diagnosis, and for the top hypothesis write the single piece of evidence that would *disprove* it. Finish by stating whether the incident had one root cause or multiple contributing factors, and name one cognitive bias you caught yourself risking.

ht1-l08-rca-report-and-post-incident-rev.title: Writing the RCA report and running a post-incident review
objectives: Structure an RCA report so any reader gets impact, cause, and fix in seconds
Build a precise incident timeline with detection, diagnosis, and resolution markers
Separate the proximate cause from the root cause and the contributing factors in writing
Write blameless language that targets systems, not individuals
Define SMART, owned, tracked corrective actions that prevent recurrence
Facilitate a post-incident review that surfaces lessons without assigning blame
ht1-l08-rca-report-and-post-incident-rev.body:
## The report is the deliverable

Your investigation only matters if others can act on it. The **RCA report** is the actual deliverable of Tier 3 work: it converts your evidence into a decision the organisation can make and a fix it can track. A brilliant diagnosis trapped in your head, or buried in 20 pages of raw logs, changes nothing.

## Structure for the reader, not the writer

Write top-down. The first thing any reader sees is a tight **executive summary**: what happened, the measurable impact, the root cause, and the fix — in seconds, not pages. Detail comes later for those who need it.

```text
RCA REPORT — INC-2026-0142
Summary   : 30 laptops lost VPN for 3h12m after the 06/14 client update.
Impact    : 30 users, ~96 user-hours lost; no data loss.
Root cause: Driver pushed without version pinning regressed the adapter.
Fix       : Pin driver version; add pre-deploy validation gate.
Status    : Mitigated 14/06; permanent fix tracked as TKT-4821.
```

State **impact in measurable terms** — users affected, duration, work or revenue lost. That is what lets leadership prioritise the fix proportionately.

## Timeline: separate detect from resolve

A good report includes a precise **timeline** with three markers: when the incident *began*, when it was *detected*, and when it was *resolved*. Splitting **time-to-detect** from **time-to-resolve** is diagnostic in itself: a long detection gap implicates your **monitoring**; a long resolution gap implicates your **runbooks, access, or tooling**. They lead to different corrective actions.

## Name the causes precisely

Use the vocabulary from this month. Separate the **proximate cause** (the immediate trigger), the **root cause** (the systemic condition), and any **contributing factors** (the other slices of cheese that aligned). If you could not prove the root cause, say so honestly: present the most-supported hypothesis with evidence for and against, the hypotheses you ruled out, the monitored mitigation, and what new data would confirm it. A **bounded unknown** preserves credibility; false certainty destroys it.

## Blameless language and SMART actions

Write **blamelessly**: assume people acted reasonably with the information they had, and target the *systems* that allowed the failure. "The tech forgot" becomes "the pipeline had no validation to catch a missing config." Blame culture hides information and guarantees recurrence.

Every report ends in **corrective actions** that are **SMART** — specific, measurable, owned, dated, and tracked:

```text
Action                              Owner       Due         Tracking
Add pre-deploy config validation    J. Okoye    2026-07-15  TKT-4821
Alert on >5 VPN drops/host/hour      S. Mensah   2026-07-08  TKT-4822
```

"Be more careful" is not an action and prevents nothing.

## Running the post-incident review

The **post-incident review (PIR)** is the meeting that turns the report into shared learning. Facilitate it **blamelessly**: walk the timeline, confirm the causes, and focus every minute on what systemic change prevents recurrence — not on who did what. Assign each action an owner and a date, and ensure they are tracked to closure. An incident with no closed actions is an incident you will have again.

## Your task

Take your most complete investigation from this month and write a one-page RCA report using the structure above: executive summary with measurable impact, a timeline that separates time-to-detect from time-to-resolve, a clear split of proximate cause / root cause / contributing factors (or an honest bounded unknown), and at least three SMART corrective actions with owner, due date, and a tracking ID. Rewrite any blame-laden sentence into blameless, systems-focused language. Finally, write a short agenda for a 30-minute post-incident review that would walk a team through it without assigning blame.

ht2-l01-powershell-deep-dive.title: PowerShell deep dive for administrators
objectives: Explain how PowerShell passes .NET objects through the pipeline rather than text
Write functions with param blocks, typed parameters, and pipeline binding
Use the streams and ErrorAction to control terminating vs non-terminating errors
Filter and shape data efficiently with Where-Object, Select-Object and calculated properties
Choose PowerShell 7 over Windows PowerShell 5.1 and understand the practical differences
Discover and read help for any cmdlet without leaving the console
ht2-l01-powershell-deep-dive.body:
## PowerShell is an object pipeline, not a text shell

If you came from Bash or `cmd`, the biggest mental shift is this: PowerShell pipes **.NET objects**, not text. When you run `Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100`, each process is a full object with properties and methods. You never parse columns by position or count spaces — you ask for the property you want.

```powershell
Get-Process |
    Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 100 } |
    Sort-Object CPU -Descending |
    Select-Object Name, Id, CPU -First 5
```

The two cmdlets you will lean on forever are **Get-Command** (find things) and **Get-Member** (see what an object actually contains). When you do not know what is on an object, pipe it to `Get-Member`.

## Functions, param blocks, and pipeline binding

Real automation lives in **functions**, not loose one-liners. A function with `[CmdletBinding()]` and a typed `param` block behaves like a built-in cmdlet — it gets `-Verbose`, `-ErrorAction`, and parameter validation for free.

```powershell
function Get-StaleDevice {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipeline)]
        [string]$DeviceName,

        [ValidateRange(1, 365)]
        [int]$StaleAfterDays = 90
    )
    process {
        Write-Verbose "Checking $DeviceName against $StaleAfterDays day window"
        # ... logic per device ...
        [pscustomobject]@{ Device = $DeviceName; StaleAfterDays = $StaleAfterDays }
    }
}
```

The `process{}` block runs once per pipeline object, so the function streams. `ValidateRange` and `ValidateSet` reject bad input before your logic ever runs.

## The error model: terminating vs non-terminating

Most cmdlets emit **non-terminating** errors that print red text but keep going — and crucially, they **slip past `try/catch`**. To trap them you must promote them with **`-ErrorAction Stop`**.

```powershell
try {
    Get-Item 'C:\does-not-exist.txt' -ErrorAction Stop
}
catch {
    Write-Warning "Handled: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
finally {
    Write-Verbose 'Cleanup runs no matter what'
}
```

PowerShell also has **streams**: success (1), error (2), warning (3), verbose (4), and information (6). Use `Write-Verbose` and `Write-Warning` instead of `Write-Host` so callers can switch detail on and off.

## Shaping data without melting your machine

Against a fleet of thousands of devices, *where* you filter matters. Filter as close to the source as possible so fewer objects travel down the pipeline.

```powershell
Get-ChildItem C:\Logs -Recurse -Filter *.log |
    Where-Object Length -gt 10MB |
    Select-Object FullName,
        @{ Name = 'SizeMB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.Length / 1MB, 1) } }
```

The `@{ Name=...; Expression=... }` syntax is a **calculated property** — it lets you rename and transform columns inline.

## PowerShell 7 vs Windows PowerShell 5.1

**Windows PowerShell 5.1** ships in the box and is in maintenance only. **PowerShell 7** is cross-platform, built on modern .NET, faster, and gets all new features — including the Microsoft Graph SDK improvements you will use this month. Install it side by side; it runs as `pwsh`.

```powershell
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion   # confirm which engine you are in
```

## Your task

Write an advanced function `Get-LargeProfile` that accepts computer profile paths from the pipeline, has a `[CmdletBinding()]` block, a mandatory `ValueFromPipeline` path parameter and a validated `-MinSizeMB` threshold (default 5000), uses a `process{}` block, emits a `[pscustomobject]` per oversized profile with a calculated `SizeGB`, and wraps its disk access in a `try/catch` with `-ErrorAction Stop`. Run it with `-Verbose` and confirm the verbose stream appears.

ht2-l02-microsoft-graph-and-sdk.title: Microsoft Graph API and the PowerShell SDK
objectives: Describe Microsoft Graph as a single REST endpoint over Entra, Intune, and M365
Install the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK and its sub-modules
Authenticate with Connect-MgGraph using the right delegated scopes
Map a Graph REST endpoint to the equivalent Get-Mg* SDK cmdlet
Page through large result sets with -All instead of truncated pages
Call endpoints the SDK has no cmdlet for using Invoke-MgGraphRequest
ht2-l02-microsoft-graph-and-sdk.body:
## One API over your whole tenant

**Microsoft Graph** is a single REST API, served from `https://graph.microsoft.com`, that exposes almost everything in your Microsoft cloud: **Entra ID** users and groups, **Intune** managed devices and policies, mail, Teams, and more. Instead of one module per product, you learn one endpoint, one permission model, and one query language (**OData**).

Everything is a resource at a URL. Users live at `/users`, managed devices at `/deviceManagement/managedDevices`, groups at `/groups`. Learn the URL pattern once and the whole API opens up.

## Installing and connecting the SDK

The **Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK** is a family of modules. Install the meta-module, or just the sub-modules you need to keep load times short.

```powershell
# Install once, for the current user
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph -Scope CurrentUser

# Or targeted sub-modules only
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.Authentication -Scope CurrentUser
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.DeviceManagement -Scope CurrentUser
```

Authentication is **scope-based**. You ask only for the **delegated scopes** your script actually uses — this is least privilege, and reviewers will check it.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All','User.Read.All'

# Confirm who you are and what you can do
(Get-MgContext).Scopes
```

If a call later returns **403 Forbidden**, your first suspect is a missing scope — check `Get-MgContext` before you blame your code.

## From REST endpoint to Get-Mg cmdlet

Every Graph endpoint maps to a typed cmdlet. The pattern is predictable: `GET /deviceManagement/managedDevices` becomes `Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice`.

```powershell
# Get every managed device, following pagination automatically
$devices = Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All

$devices |
    Where-Object { $_.OperatingSystem -eq 'Windows' } |
    Select-Object DeviceName, OsVersion, LastSyncDateTime
```

The **`-All`** switch matters. Without it, Graph returns just the first page and silently follows an `@odata.nextLink` for the rest; `-All` walks every page so you do not miss devices.

## OData query options keep payloads small

Do not pull whole objects and filter in PowerShell when Graph can do it server-side. Use `-Filter`, `-Select`, and `-Top`.

```powershell
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All `
    -Filter "operatingSystem eq 'Windows'" `
    -Property 'deviceName,osVersion,complianceState' |
    Select-Object DeviceName, OsVersion, ComplianceState
```

Server-side filtering means less data over the wire and fewer throttling problems on big tenants.

## Invoke-MgGraphRequest for anything the cmdlets miss

New features land in the **beta** endpoint first, and not every action has a typed cmdlet. **`Invoke-MgGraphRequest`** sends a raw authenticated request to any Graph URI and reuses your existing token.

```powershell
$uri = 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/managedDevices?$top=5'
$response = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri
$response.value | Select-Object deviceName, osVersion

# It also works for actions:
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method POST `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/{id}/rebootNow'
```

This is your escape hatch — when the SDK has no cmdlet, the REST call always works.

## Your task

Connect to Graph with the minimum scopes needed to read managed devices. Write a function `Get-IntuneDeviceInventory` that retrieves **all** managed devices with `-All`, uses server-side `-Filter` and `-Property` to return only Windows devices and only the `deviceName`, `osVersion`, and `lastSyncDateTime` fields, and exports the result to CSV. Then re-implement the same read using `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` against the v1.0 endpoint and confirm the two approaches return the same count.

ht2-l03-automating-intune-and-entra.title: Automating Intune and Entra with Graph
objectives: Query Intune managed devices and trigger device actions through Graph
Manage Entra ID users and group memberships programmatically
Resolve a device or user object to its Graph id before acting on it
Drive dynamic vs assigned group membership and understand the difference
Add ShouldProcess so bulk scripts support -WhatIf and -Confirm
Throttle-proof a bulk operation with batching and Retry-After handling
ht2-l03-automating-intune-and-entra.body:
## Acting on Intune devices, not just reading them

Reading inventory is half the job. The other half is **taking action** — sync, restart, retire, or wipe a device. Graph actions target a resource by its **id** in the URL, so the workflow is always: resolve to id, then act.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementManagedDevices.PrivilegedOperations.All','DeviceManagementManagedDevices.ReadWrite.All'

# Resolve the device to its Graph id
$device = Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All `
    -Filter "deviceName eq 'LAP-0427'"

# Trigger a sync action against that id
Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId $device.Id
```

Privileged actions like wipe require a stronger scope (`PrivilegedOperations.All`). Request it only in scripts that genuinely need it.

## Managing Entra users and groups

The same SDK manages **Entra ID**. Users, groups, and the relationships between them are all Graph resources.

```powershell
# Resolve a user to their stable object id
$user = Get-MgUser -Filter "userPrincipalName eq 'jdoe@contoso.com'"

# Add that user to a group by id
New-MgGroupMember -GroupId $groupId -DirectoryObjectId $user.Id
```

Always act on the **object id**, not the `userPrincipalName`. UPNs get renamed; the id never changes and relationship endpoints expect it.

## Dynamic vs assigned groups

An **assigned group** is one you add and remove members from by hand (or by script). A **dynamic group** recalculates its membership from a **membership rule** — for example, all Windows devices. You manage assigned groups with `New-MgGroupMember`; you manage dynamic ones by editing the rule.

```powershell
# A dynamic device group: rule, not manual members
$params = @{
    DisplayName     = 'All Windows Devices'
    MailEnabled     = $false
    MailNickname    = 'allWinDevices'
    SecurityEnabled = $true
    GroupTypes      = @('DynamicMembership')
    MembershipRule  = '(device.deviceOSType -eq "Windows")'
    MembershipRuleProcessingState = 'On'
}
New-MgGroup @params
```

## Make bulk changes safe with ShouldProcess

A script that loops over hundreds of devices must support a **dry run**. Adding `SupportsShouldProcess` to `[CmdletBinding()]` gives your function free `-WhatIf` and `-Confirm`.

```powershell
function Invoke-DeviceSyncBulk {
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess, ConfirmImpact = 'High')]
    param([Parameter(Mandatory)][object[]]$Devices)
    process {
        foreach ($d in $Devices) {
            if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($d.DeviceName, 'Sync device')) {
                Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId $d.Id
            }
        }
    }
}
# Preview first, then commit:
Invoke-DeviceSyncBulk -Devices $stale -WhatIf
```

## Surviving throttling at scale

Graph throttles aggressive callers with **HTTP 429**. The response carries a **`Retry-After`** header telling you how long to pause. Honour it, ideally with backoff.

```powershell
foreach ($d in $devices) {
    try {
        Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId $d.Id -ErrorAction Stop
    }
    catch {
        if ($_.Exception.Response.StatusCode -eq 429) {
            $wait = [int]($_.Exception.Response.Headers.RetryAfter.Delta.TotalSeconds)
            Start-Sleep -Seconds ($wait ? $wait : 10)
        }
        else { throw }
    }
}
```

## Your task

Write a function `Set-StaleDeviceGroup` that finds all managed devices whose `lastSyncDateTime` is older than 30 days, resolves each to its id, and adds them to a specified assigned Entra group. Support `-WhatIf` via `SupportsShouldProcess`, request only the scopes you need, and wrap the group-add call in a try/catch that honours `Retry-After` on a 429. Run it once with `-WhatIf` to prove the preview works before any change is made.

ht2-l04-intune-proactive-remediations.title: Intune proactive remediations
objectives: Explain the detection-plus-remediation script pair model and its exit-code contract
Write a detection script that exits 1 only when remediation is needed
Write a matching remediation script that fixes the issue idempotently
Understand the SYSTEM vs user context and 64-bit execution settings
Interpret detection and remediation status output in the Intune reports
Deploy a remediation to a device group and read pre/post remediation results
ht2-l04-intune-proactive-remediations.body:
## Self-healing endpoints, by design

A **proactive remediation** (now called a **remediation** in Intune) is a pair of PowerShell scripts that run on a schedule via the **Intune Management Extension**: a **detection** script that decides whether a problem exists, and a **remediation** script that fixes it. The two scripts communicate through a strict **exit-code contract**.

- Detection **exit 0** = healthy, do nothing.
- Detection **exit 1** = problem found, run the remediation.

This pair model lets you first *measure* how widespread an issue is across the fleet before you ever change a device.

## Writing the detection script

Detection should be fast, read-only, and decisive. Output a short status string (it appears in the Intune report), then exit with the right code.

```powershell
# Detect: is the Windows Time service running and automatic?
$svc = Get-Service -Name 'W32Time' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

if ($svc -and $svc.Status -eq 'Running' -and $svc.StartType -eq 'Automatic') {
    Write-Output 'W32Time healthy: running and automatic'
    exit 0
}
else {
    Write-Output 'W32Time not running or not automatic'
    exit 1
}
```

The **last line on stdout** becomes the *pre-remediation output* in reporting, so make it human-readable.

## Writing the remediation script

Remediation must be **idempotent** — running it on an already-fixed device must be harmless and produce the same end state. Always wrap changes in `try/catch` and exit non-zero on failure so Intune records the failure.

```powershell
try {
    Set-Service -Name 'W32Time' -StartupType Automatic -ErrorAction Stop
    Start-Service -Name 'W32Time' -ErrorAction Stop
    Write-Output 'W32Time set to Automatic and started'
    exit 0
}
catch {
    Write-Output "Remediation failed: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    exit 1
}
```

Because this runs on a schedule, re-running on a healthy device simply re-asserts the desired state with no harm.

## Context and bitness matter

Two settings change behaviour. **Run this script using the logged-on credentials** controls whether the script runs as the user (needed for `HKCU` and per-user settings) or as **SYSTEM** (the default, for machine-wide changes). **Run script in 64-bit PowerShell** should be **Yes** whenever you touch 64-bit registry hives or program paths — otherwise the script runs 32-bit and gets redirected to `WOW6432Node`, hiding the real state.

## Deploying and reading results

You assign a remediation to a **device or user group** with a schedule (once, hourly, or daily). Intune then shows, per device, the detection status and remediation status. You can also manage remediations through Graph as `deviceHealthScript` resources.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All'

# List your remediation (device health) scripts via Graph
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/deviceHealthScripts' |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty value |
    Select-Object displayName, id
```

Start with **detection only** (a remediation that just reports) to size the problem, then add the fix and pilot it on a small ring.

## Your task

Build a complete remediation pair for a real issue: a stale DNS cache or a disabled firewall profile (your choice). The **detection** script must read-only check the condition, write a clear single-line status, and exit 0 or 1 correctly. The **remediation** script must fix it **idempotently**, wrap changes in `try/catch`, and exit 0 on success and 1 on failure. State which context (SYSTEM or user) and bitness it needs and why. Finally, use `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` to list the `deviceHealthScripts` in your tenant.

ht2-l05-configuration-as-code.title: Configuration as code for endpoints
objectives: Explain why endpoint configuration should be declarative, versioned code
Export an existing Intune policy as JSON via Graph
Store policy definitions in Git and review changes through pull requests
Write an idempotent import that creates or updates a policy by name
Separate environment-specific values from policy templates
Understand the IntuneCM / community tooling landscape for config as code
ht2-l05-configuration-as-code.body:
## Why configuration should be code

Clicking through the Intune portal works for one device, once. It does not scale, it leaves no history, and a wrong click can hit thousands of endpoints. **Configuration as code** treats your **desired state** as declarative files — JSON policy definitions — kept in **Git** and deployed by automation. You gain a diffable **audit trail**, **peer review** through pull requests, and **rollback** to any prior commit.

The mental model: the repo is the source of truth, and Intune is just the runtime that the repo deploys to.

## Export what you already have

Start by capturing your current state. Graph exposes configuration profiles as resources you can `GET` and serialise to JSON.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementConfiguration.Read.All'

$policies = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/configurationPolicies' |
    Select-Object -ExpandProperty value

foreach ($p in $policies) {
    $safe = $p.name -replace '[^\w\-]', '_'
    $p | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content ".\policies\$safe.json" -Encoding UTF8
}
```

Commit that `policies` folder to Git. You now have a baseline you can diff against forever.

## Idempotent import: create or update by name

The heart of config as code is an import that is **safe to re-run**. It looks the policy up by a stable key — usually `displayName` or `name` — then **updates** it if it exists and **creates** it if it does not.

```powershell
function Import-IntunePolicy {
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]
    param([Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Path)

    $def  = Get-Content $Path -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
    $base = 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/configurationPolicies'

    $existing = (Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET `
        -Uri "$base?`$filter=name eq '$($def.name)'").value

    if ($existing) {
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($def.name, 'Update policy')) {
            Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method PATCH `
                -Uri "$base/$($existing[0].id)" -Body ($def | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20)
        }
    }
    else {
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($def.name, 'Create policy')) {
            Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method POST `
                -Uri $base -Body ($def | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20)
        }
    }
}
```

Run it twice; the second run changes nothing. That is the property you want.

## Separate templates from environment values

Never hard-code tenant or group ids inside a policy template. Keep them in a **parameter file** per environment and inject at deploy time, so the *same* template promotes from **dev** to **prod** by swapping one file.

```powershell
$env = Get-Content '.\envs\prod.json' -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json
$template = (Get-Content '.\templates\baseline.json' -Raw) `
    -replace '{{TargetGroupId}}', $env.TargetGroupId
```

## The tooling landscape

You can write your own importer, or stand on community tooling. Projects like the **IntuneCM** family and Microsoft's own samples wrap this export/import/assign loop with backup and reporting. Whatever you use, the principles are identical: declarative files, Git review, idempotent deploy.

## Your task

Build a minimal config-as-code pipeline by hand. Export at least two Intune **configurationPolicies** to JSON and commit them. Write an idempotent `Import-IntunePolicy` function (create-or-update by name, with `SupportsShouldProcess`). Move one environment-specific value — a target group id — out of the template into a per-environment JSON file and inject it at deploy time. Demonstrate a re-run that reports *no changes* the second time, and capture the `-WhatIf` output as proof of a safe dry run.

ht2-l07-azure-automation-runbooks.title: Scheduled automation and runbooks with Azure Automation
objectives: Explain what Azure Automation runbooks are and when to use them over local scripts
Authenticate a runbook to Graph using a managed identity instead of stored secrets
Grant a managed identity the exact Graph application permissions it needs
Import modules into the Automation account and pin versions
Schedule a runbook and pass parameters at run time
Capture output, errors, and verbose streams in job logs for operations
ht2-l07-azure-automation-runbooks.body:
## Why run automation in the cloud

A script that only works when *you* run it on *your* laptop is not automation — it is a chore with extra steps. **Azure Automation** hosts your PowerShell as **runbooks** that run unattended on Azure compute, on a **schedule** or trigger, with no machine to leave switched on and no one to remember to click run.

Use runbooks for anything recurring at fleet scale: nightly stale-device reports, scheduled group hygiene, off-hours remediation sweeps.

## Authenticate without secrets: managed identity

The worst thing you can do is paste a credential into a script. A **managed identity** is an Azure-managed credential attached to the Automation account; Azure rotates it and you never see it. The Graph SDK connects to it with one switch.

```powershell
# Inside the runbook — no secret, no prompt
Connect-MgGraph -Identity -NoWelcome

$context = Get-MgContext
Write-Output "Connected as $($context.AppName) in tenant $($context.TenantId)"
```

Because the runbook runs **as itself** with no signed-in user, it uses **application permissions**, not delegated ones.

## Grant the identity exactly what it needs

You grant the managed identity specific **Graph application permissions** (app roles) — and only those. This is least privilege at the identity level. The grant itself can be scripted.

```powershell
# Run once by an admin to grant the runbook's identity a Graph app role
$graphSp   = Get-MgServicePrincipal -Filter "appId eq '00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000'"
$miSp      = Get-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId $managedIdentityObjectId
$appRole   = $graphSp.AppRoles | Where-Object { $_.Value -eq 'DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All' }

New-MgServicePrincipalAppRoleAssignment -ServicePrincipalId $miSp.Id `
    -PrincipalId $miSp.Id -ResourceId $graphSp.Id -AppRoleId $appRole.Id
```

## Modules and version pinning

A runbook can only use modules **imported into the Automation account**. Import the Graph sub-modules you need and **pin their versions** so a surprise update never breaks a scheduled job at 2 a.m.

```powershell
# The runbook body declares what it expects; the account provides it
#Requires -Modules @{ ModuleName='Microsoft.Graph.Authentication'; ModuleVersion='2.0.0' }
#Requires -Modules @{ ModuleName='Microsoft.Graph.DeviceManagement'; ModuleVersion='2.0.0' }
```

Import modules via the portal, or programmatically with `New-AzAutomationModule`.

## Schedule, parameterise, and log

Attach a **schedule** (daily, weekly, or a recurring interval) and pass **parameters** at run time so one runbook serves many cases. Because there is no console, design for the **job log**: every `Write-Output`, `Write-Error`, and `Write-Verbose` is captured per job.

```powershell
param(
    [int]$StaleDays = 30,
    [string]$OutputContainerUrl
)
Connect-MgGraph -Identity -NoWelcome

$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddDays(-$StaleDays)
$stale  = Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All |
    Where-Object { $_.LastSyncDateTime -lt $cutoff }

Write-Output "Found $($stale.Count) devices stale beyond $StaleDays days"
$stale | Select-Object DeviceName, LastSyncDateTime | ConvertTo-Json
```

Review the per-job streams in the Automation account's **job history** to confirm what ran and catch failures.

## Your task

Design (and where you have a sandbox, build) a runbook `Report-StaleDevices` that authenticates with `Connect-MgGraph -Identity`, accepts a `-StaleDays` parameter, lists every device stale beyond that window, and writes a JSON summary to `Write-Output`. List the **exact** Graph application permission its managed identity needs and why. Add `#Requires` lines pinning the Graph module versions, and attach a daily schedule. Describe where you would read the job log to verify the run and how you would alert on failure.

ht3-l01-zero-trust-for-endpoints.title: Zero Trust architecture for endpoints
objectives: Explain the three Zero Trust principles and why implicit trust by network location is obsolete
'Map the Zero Trust pillars to endpoint controls: identity, device, app, data, network'
Describe how device compliance state becomes a signal in an access decision
Differentiate authentication, authorization and continuous access evaluation at the endpoint
Design a high-level Zero Trust enforcement flow for a managed Windows device
Identify the telemetry sources that feed endpoint trust decisions
ht3-l01-zero-trust-for-endpoints.body:
## The perimeter is gone

For decades security assumed a hard shell and a soft centre: get past the firewall or onto the VPN, and you were trusted. Cloud apps, remote work and BYOD destroyed that model. **Zero Trust** replaces it with three principles: **verify explicitly**, use **least-privilege access**, and **assume breach**. Network location is no longer a trust signal. Every request — including from a device sitting in your own office — must be authenticated, authorized and validated against current signals.

For an endpoint engineer this is a mindset shift. The device stops being a passive client and becomes an active participant whose **health and compliance state** feed directly into whether access is granted.

## The pillars and how endpoints touch each

Microsoft's Zero Trust model spans **Identity, Devices, Applications, Data, Network** and Infrastructure. An endpoint sits at the intersection:

- **Identity** — the user and the device both have identities (the device identity comes from Entra join or hybrid join).
- **Devices** — compliance policy decides if the endpoint is healthy: encrypted, patched, EDR-onboarded, not jailbroken.
- **Applications** — app protection policies and managed app access.
- **Data** — encryption at rest (BitLocker) and labelling/DLP in transit.
- **Network** — segmentation so a compromised endpoint cannot roam.

## Compliance state as a signal

The heart of endpoint Zero Trust is that **device compliance becomes an input to authorization**. Intune evaluates a device against policy and stamps it compliant or non-compliant. **Conditional Access** then consumes that state. A simplified decision flow looks like this:

```text
User + device request access to resource
  -> Authenticate user (MFA / passwordless)
  -> Evaluate signals: user risk, sign-in risk, device compliance, location, app
  -> Decision: Grant / Grant with controls / Block
  -> Continuously re-evaluate (CAE) for revocation & risk change
```

Notice authorization is **not** a one-time gate. With **Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)** a disabled account, a password reset or a sudden risk spike can revoke a live session in near real time, instead of waiting for a token to expire.

## Least privilege at the endpoint

Assume breach means scoping access tightly. On the endpoint that translates to removing standing local-admin rights, using **just-in-time** elevation, and applying **just-enough-access**. You can confirm a user is not a standing admin:

```powershell
# List members of the local Administrators group
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators' |
  Select-Object Name, PrincipalSource, ObjectClass
```

Every account that does not strictly need elevation is removed. A compromised standard user is far less useful to an attacker than a compromised admin.

## Telemetry feeds the decision

Zero Trust only works if the signals are trustworthy and current. Endpoint telemetry — sign-in logs, **Defender for Endpoint** alerts, Intune compliance, and device risk scores — flows into the policy engine. The richer and fresher the signal, the better the decision. This is why EDR onboarding and compliance reporting are not optional extras; they are the sensory system of your access control.

## Your task

For one managed Windows device in a test tenant, document its full Zero Trust posture: device join type, compliance policy result, BitLocker and EDR onboarding state, and the local Administrators membership. Then draw the access-decision flow for that device reaching a sensitive app, naming every signal Conditional Access would evaluate and where CAE would intervene on a revocation event.

ht3-l02-advanced-conditional-access.title: Advanced Conditional Access and risk-based policies
objectives: Break a Conditional Access policy into its assignments and access controls and explain what each lever
