Never post a template with placeholder text or default branding still visible.

## Adding a Clear Call-to-Action (CTA)

Most marketing graphics need an action: *Shop Now*, *Learn More*, *Swipe Up*, *Link in Bio*. Make the CTA visually distinct using a button shape or contrasting color.

## Exporting Correctly

- **PNG**: best for graphics with text and crisp edges.
- **JPG**: smaller files, good for photo-heavy posts.
- **MP4/GIF**: for animated posts or stories.

Name files clearly (e.g., `IG_post_summer-sale_2024-06.png`) and organize them in dated folders for easy reuse.

## Quick Production Workflow

1. Pick correct size.
2. Apply brand kit.
3. Choose/adapt a template.
4. Add headline, supporting text, and CTA following hierarchy.
5. Check alignment, contrast, spacing.
6. Export in the right format and name the file.

dm-m1-l04-producing-short-form-video-for.title: Producing Short-Form Video for Reels, TikTok & Shorts
objectives: Explain why short-form vertical video drives reach and engagement across Reels, TikTok, and Shorts
Write a scroll-stopping hook that captures attention in the first 3 seconds
Plan a short-form video using a simple shot list and trending format
Film clean vertical footage on a phone using basic lighting, framing, and audio best practices
Edit a finished video in a mobile app with captions, trending audio, and on-screen text
Apply platform-specific best practices for posting, hashtags, and captions
dm-m1-l04-producing-short-form-video-for.body:
## Why Short-Form Video Matters

Short-form vertical video (typically 9:16, 15-90 seconds) is the highest-reach content format on social media today. Platforms like TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts actively push this format because it keeps users on the app longer. For a junior social media assistant, knowing how to produce these videos quickly and consistently is one of the most valuable skills you can offer.

Key reasons short-form works:

- **Algorithmic reach**: Platforms show Reels/TikToks/Shorts to non-followers, so even small accounts can go viral.
- **Low production cost**: A phone is enough — no expensive gear required.
- **High engagement**: Quick, entertaining content drives comments, shares, and saves.

## The Most Important Metric: Watch Time & Retention

The algorithm rewards videos that keep people watching. Two metrics matter most:

- **Average watch time / completion rate** — how much of the video people watch.
- **Re-watches and shares** — strong signals of quality.

Everything in your video should serve one goal: keep the viewer watching to the end.

## The Hook (First 3 Seconds)

The hook is the single most important part of any short-form video. If you don't grab attention immediately, viewers swipe away.

Types of strong hooks:

- **Question hook**: "Why is no one talking about this?"
- **Bold statement**: "You're using this app wrong."
- **Visual hook**: Show the most surprising/satisfying moment first.
- **Curiosity gap**: "Wait until you see what happens at the end."
- **Relatable callout**: "If you're a small business owner, stop scrolling."

Pair a verbal hook with an on-screen text hook so it works even with the sound off.

## Trending Formats

You rarely need to invent something new. Adapt proven formats to your brand:

- **Trending audio**: Use sounds that are currently rising. On TikTok and Reels, trending audio boosts reach.
- **Listicles**: "3 tools every marketer needs."
- **Before/after**: Transformation reveals.
- **POV / storytelling**: Put the viewer in a scenario.
- **Tutorials / how-to**: Quick value-packed steps.
- **Talking head**: You or a presenter speaking directly to camera with captions.

## Planning Your Video

Before filming, write a simple plan:

1. **Goal**: What action or feeling do you want? (Follow, save, visit link)
2. **Hook**: Your first line and first frame.
3. **Shot list**: Bullet each clip you need.
4. **Script / talking points**: Keep it tight — short-form has no room for waffle.
5. **Call to action (CTA)**: "Follow for more," "Comment your question."

Example shot list:

```
Hook: close-up, "Stop wasting money on ads"
Shot 1: screen recording of analytics
Shot 2: talking head explaining tip
Shot 3: result / before-after
CTA: "Follow for daily tips"
```

## Filming on a Phone

You don't need a studio. Follow these basics:

- **Orientation**: Always film vertical (9:16).
- **Lighting**: Face a window or use a ring light. Avoid backlighting.
- **Framing**: Keep your subject centred, leave room for captions top and bottom.
- **Stability**: Use a tripod or prop your phone up.
- **Audio**: Film in a quiet room; a cheap clip-on mic improves clarity hugely.
- **Shoot extra**: Capture a few takes and some b-roll for editing flexibility.

## Editing with Mobile Tools

Free apps make editing fast: **CapCut**, **InShot**, or the native in-app editors in TikTok and Instagram.

Editing checklist:

- **Cut tight**: Remove pauses and dead air to keep pace fast.
- **Add captions**: Use auto-captions — most viewers watch on mute. Always check for errors.
- **On-screen text**: Reinforce key points and the hook.
- **Trending audio**: Add it inside the native app so the platform recognises it.
- **Pacing**: Change shots/visuals every few seconds to hold attention.
- **Keep it short**: Trim anything that doesn't add value.

## Posting Best Practices

- **Caption**: Short, with a hook or question to drive comments.
- **Hashtags**: Mix a few relevant niche and broad tags (3-5 is plenty).
- **Cover/thumbnail**: Choose a clear frame with text for the grid.
- **Timing**: Post when your audience is active; check insights.
- **Native upload**: Post directly in-app; avoid visible watermarks from other apps (e.g. TikTok logo on Reels can reduce reach).

## Workflow Summary

Plan → Hook → Film vertical → Edit tight with captions → Add trending audio → Post natively with a strong caption and CTA → Review analytics → Repeat what works.

dm-m2-l01-campaign-planning-setting-smar.title: Campaign Planning & Setting SMART Objectives
objectives: Explain why a written campaign brief is essential before spending ad budget
Apply the SMART framework to turn vague marketing wishes into measurable objectives
Identify and define a target audience using demographics, interests, and intent
Match campaign goals to the correct objective type on Meta and Google Ads
Set a realistic budget and choose channels that fit the goal and audience
Produce a complete one-page campaign brief ready for client or manager sign-off
dm-m2-l01-campaign-planning-setting-smar.body:
## Why plan before you spend?

Paid advertising is the one area of marketing where mistakes cost real money immediately. A poorly planned campaign burns budget on the wrong people, with the wrong message, chasing a goal nobody agreed on. A **campaign brief** is the cheap insurance against that: a single document everyone signs off on before a cent is spent.

A good brief answers five questions:

1. **Why** are we running this? (the business goal)
2. **Who** are we trying to reach? (the audience)
3. **Where** will we reach them? (the channels)
4. **How much** can we spend, and over what period? (budget & timeline)
5. **What** does success look like, in numbers? (the SMART objective)

## The SMART framework

Vague goals like "get more sales" or "grow our following" can never be judged a success or failure. SMART turns them into something you can measure.

- **S — Specific:** What exactly do you want? (e.g. newsletter sign-ups, not "engagement")
- **M — Measurable:** Attach a number you can track in the ad platform or analytics.
- **A — Achievable:** Realistic given the budget, audience size, and timeframe.
- **R — Relevant:** Tied to a real business outcome, not a vanity metric.
- **T — Time-bound:** A clear deadline or campaign window.

**Weak goal:** "Get more website visitors."

**SMART goal:** "Drive 1,500 new website visitors from Australia aged 25–40 to our spring sale page within 30 days, at a cost per click under $0.80, for a total spend of $1,000."

## Defining your audience

Knowing who you're targeting shapes every other decision. Build your audience from three angles:

- **Demographics:** age, gender, location, language, job title.
- **Interests & behaviours:** hobbies, pages they follow, purchase behaviour (Meta excels here).
- **Intent:** what they're actively searching for (Google Search excels here).

A quick **audience persona** helps: give them a name, a problem, and a reason to click. "Budget-conscious Bianca, 32, searching 'cheap running shoes Melbourne'."

## Choosing channels: Meta vs Google

- **Google Search Ads** capture *existing demand*—people already searching for what you offer. Great for high-intent, bottom-of-funnel goals like purchases and leads.
- **Meta Ads (Facebook/Instagram)** *create demand*—they interrupt people based on interests. Great for awareness, discovery, and visually appealing products.
- Many campaigns use both: Meta to build awareness, Google to capture the resulting searches.

## Matching goals to platform objectives

Both platforms make you pick a campaign objective up front, and the algorithm optimises around it. Choose wrong and you waste budget.

- **Awareness / Reach** → top of funnel (Meta Awareness, Google Display/Video).
- **Traffic / Consideration** → mid funnel (Meta Traffic or Engagement, Google Search clicks).
- **Leads / Sales / Conversions** → bottom of funnel (Meta Sales, Google Performance Max or Search with conversions).

## Setting a budget

- Start with the total you can afford, then work backwards: `budget ÷ target cost-per-result = expected results`.
- Distinguish **daily budget** (spend per day) from **lifetime budget** (total over the campaign).
- Always leave room for a **testing phase**—the first few days teach the algorithm and you.

## The campaign brief template

Put it all on one page:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Campaign name | Spring Sale 2025 |
| Business goal | Increase online sales |
| SMART objective | 50 purchases in 30 days at ≤$15 cost-per-purchase |
| Audience | Women 25–45, Australia, interested in fitness |
| Channels | Meta (Instagram), Google Search |
| Budget | $750 total ($25/day) |
| Timeline | 1–30 September |
| Key message | 20% off all activewear |
| Success metric | Cost per purchase, total revenue (ROAS) |

Get this signed off, and you're ready to build the campaign with confidence.

dm-m2-l02-launching-your-first-meta-ads-.title: Launching Your First Meta Ads Campaign
objectives: Navigate Meta Ads Manager and explain the campaign, ad set, and ad hierarchy
Select the correct campaign objective based on a business goal
Build saved, custom, and lookalike audiences with appropriate targeting
Set daily vs lifetime budgets and choose placements
Create compliant ad creative and publish a Facebook/Instagram campaign
Identify key metrics to monitor after launch
dm-m2-l02-launching-your-first-meta-ads-.body:
## Why Meta Ads?

Meta (Facebook + Instagram) reaches billions of users daily and offers granular targeting at low entry cost. As a junior assistant, you'll often be asked to launch and monitor simple campaigns, so mastering Ads Manager is essential.

## The Three-Level Structure

Every Meta campaign uses a strict hierarchy:

1. **Campaign** — where you set the *objective* (what you want to achieve).
2. **Ad Set** — where you define *audience, budget, schedule, and placements*.
3. **Ad** — the actual *creative* (image/video, copy, headline, link, call-to-action).

A single campaign can hold multiple ad sets, and each ad set can hold multiple ads. This lets you test audiences and creatives systematically.

## Step 1 — Set Up Ads Manager

- You need a **Facebook Business Page** and a **Meta Business Suite / Business Manager** account.
- Add a **payment method** under Billing.
- Confirm your Page and ad account permissions before building.

## Step 2 — Choose the Right Objective

Meta groups objectives by funnel stage:

| Objective | Use when you want… |
|---|---|
| Awareness | Maximum reach / brand visibility |
| Traffic | Clicks to a website or app |
| Engagement | Likes, comments, messages, video views |
| Leads | Form fills, sign-ups |
| App promotion | App installs |
| Sales | Conversions / purchases (needs the Meta Pixel) |

**Rule of thumb:** match the objective to the *business goal*, not to vanity metrics. Choosing 'Sales' tells Meta's algorithm to find buyers, not just clickers.

## Step 3 — Define Your Audience

Three audience types you'll use most:

- **Saved (Core) audiences** — built from location, age, gender, interests, and behaviours.
- **Custom audiences** — people who already know you: website visitors (via Pixel), customer email lists, video viewers, page engagers.
- **Lookalike audiences** — Meta finds new people similar to a custom audience (e.g., 1% lookalike of your best customers).

Keep audiences broad enough to deliver (avoid over-narrowing) but relevant. Watch the **audience size estimate** indicator.

## Step 4 — Budget & Schedule

- **Daily budget**: average amount spent per day — good for ongoing campaigns.
- **Lifetime budget**: total spend across the whole run — good for fixed promotions; allows ad scheduling (dayparting).
- Start small (e.g., £5–£10/day) to gather data before scaling.
- Meta uses an **auction**; you usually let it bid automatically (Highest Volume) when starting out.

## Step 5 — Placements

- **Advantage+ placements (automatic)** is recommended for beginners — Meta distributes across Feeds, Stories, Reels, etc.
- Use **Manual placements** only when you have a specific reason (e.g., Instagram-only creative).

## Step 6 — Build the Ad Creative

- Choose a format: single image, video, or carousel.
- Write clear **primary text**, a punchy **headline**, and a relevant **call-to-action** button.
- Use a strong destination URL and add **UTM parameters** for tracking.
- Follow image specs (e.g., 1080×1080 square or 1080×1350 vertical for feeds/Reels).

## Step 7 — Review, Publish, Monitor

- Check Ads Manager warnings, then click **Publish**. Ads enter **review** (usually within 24 hours).
- After launch, watch: **Reach, Impressions, CPM, CTR, CPC, Results, and Cost per Result**.
- Let campaigns exit the **learning phase** (~50 conversions/week) before judging performance; avoid editing too soon.

## Policy & Compliance Notes

- Avoid prohibited content and respect ad policies (no misleading claims, restricted categories).
- Sensitive categories (housing, employment, credit) require **Special Ad Categories** with limited targeting.

## Quick Launch Checklist

1. Objective matches goal
2. Audience defined and sized
3. Budget set (start small)
4. Placements chosen
5. Creative + copy + CTA + URL ready
6. Tracking (Pixel/UTMs) in place
7. Review warnings → Publish

dm-m2-l03-running-search-campaigns-with-.title: Running Search Campaigns with Google Ads
objectives: Explain how Google Search ads work and the role of the ad auction and Quality Score
Structure a campaign into themed ad groups with relevant keywords
Select appropriate keyword match types and add negative keywords
Write compelling responsive search ads with strong headlines, descriptions, and assets
Set budgets, bidding strategies, and conversion tracking to measure results
dm-m2-l03-running-search-campaigns-with-.body:
## Why Search Campaigns Matter

Google Search campaigns show text ads to people who are *actively searching* for what you offer. Because the user has high intent (they typed the query), search ads often deliver strong return on ad spend. Your job as a junior assistant is to make sure the right ad shows for the right query at the right cost.

## How the Search Auction Works

Every time someone searches, Google runs an instant auction. Your ad position and cost depend on **Ad Rank**, which combines:

- **Your bid** – the maximum you'll pay for a click
- **Quality Score** – Google's 1-10 rating based on expected click-through rate, ad relevance, and landing page experience
- **Ad assets and formats** – extensions and other enhancements

A higher Quality Score means you can rank higher while paying *less* per click. So relevance is not just good practice — it saves money.

## Account Structure

Good structure keeps ads relevant and easy to manage:

```
Account
 └── Campaign (budget, location, bidding)
      └── Ad Group (one theme / keyword set)
           ├── Keywords
           └── Responsive Search Ads
```

**Rule of thumb:** one tight theme per ad group. For a shoe shop, don't mix "running shoes" and "hiking boots" in one ad group. Split them so each ad group's ads and keywords match.

## Keywords and Match Types

Match types control how closely a search must match your keyword:

- **Broad match** `running shoes` – widest reach, can trigger loosely related searches. Use with smart bidding and watch closely.
- **Phrase match** `"running shoes"` – searches that include the meaning of the phrase.
- **Exact match** `[running shoes]` – searches with the same meaning as the keyword. Tightest control.

**Negative keywords** stop your ads showing for irrelevant terms (e.g. add `free`, `jobs`, `repair` if you don't want those). Review the **Search Terms report** regularly to find new negatives and new keyword ideas.

## Writing Responsive Search Ads (RSAs)

RSAs let you supply up to **15 headlines** and **4 descriptions**; Google mixes them to find top combinations.

Best practices:

- Include your main keyword in at least 2-3 headlines for relevance
- Add benefits, offers, and a clear **call to action** ("Shop Now", "Get a Free Quote")
- Make headlines distinct so combinations don't repeat
- Pin sparingly — pinning a headline to position 1 limits Google's testing
- Aim for an **Ad Strength** of "Good" or "Excellent"

## Ad Assets (Extensions)

Add assets to take up more space and give users more reasons to click:

- **Sitelinks** – links to specific pages
- **Callouts** – short phrases like "Free Delivery"
- **Structured snippets** – lists (e.g. Brands, Services)
- **Call asset** – phone number

## Budgets, Bidding & Conversions

- Set a realistic **daily budget**; Google may spend up to 2x on a given day but balances over the month.
- Start with **Maximise Clicks** to gather data, then move to **Maximise Conversions** or **Target CPA/ROAS** once conversion tracking has data.
- **Conversion tracking is essential** — without it, smart bidding is blind and you can't prove results.

## A Simple Build Checklist

1. Define the goal (sales, leads, calls).
2. Set campaign settings: networks (Search only to start), locations, languages, budget, bidding.
3. Create ad groups by theme.
4. Add 5-15 keywords per ad group with chosen match types.
5. Write 2-3 RSAs per ad group; aim for good Ad Strength.
6. Add assets/extensions.
7. Add negative keywords.
8. Confirm conversion tracking is live, then launch and monitor.

dm-m2-l04-optimizing-ad-performance-a-b-.title: Optimizing Ad Performance & A/B Testing
objectives: Identify and interpret the core paid ad metrics (CTR, CPC, CPM, CPR, ROAS, conversion rate) on Meta
dm-m2-l04-optimizing-ad-performance-a-b-.body:
## Why optimization matters

Launching an ad is only the start. The real job of a Social Media Assistant is to **monitor, test, and improve** so the same budget delivers more results. Optimization is about lowering your **cost-per-result** (CPR) — the cost of each click, lead, or sale — while keeping quality high.

## The metrics that matter

Don't drown in numbers. Focus on metrics tied to your objective.

- **Impressions** — how many times the ad was shown.
- **CTR (Click-Through Rate)** — clicks ÷ impressions. Signals whether the creative/offer grabs attention. Benchmark: ~1%+ on Meta, ~2%+ on Google Search.
- **CPC (Cost Per Click)** — what you pay per click. Lower is better if click quality holds.
- **CPM (Cost Per Mille)** — cost per 1,000 impressions. Reflects audience competition and ad quality.
- **Conversion Rate** — conversions ÷ clicks. Signals whether the landing page/offer delivers.
- **CPR / CPA (Cost Per Result / Acquisition)** — the bottom-line efficiency metric.
- **ROAS (Return on Ad Spend)** — revenue ÷ spend. Key for e-commerce.

### Reading the signals

| Symptom | Likely cause | First fix |
|---|---|---|
| Low CTR | Weak creative or wrong audience | Test new hook/image |
| High CTR but low conversions | Landing page or offer mismatch | Improve page/offer |
| Rising CPM | Audience too narrow or ad fatigue | Refresh creative, widen audience |
| High CPR overall | Inefficient targeting or bidding | Restructure or A/B test |

## What is A/B testing?

A/B testing (split testing) compares **two versions that differ by ONE variable** to see which performs better. Changing one thing at a time is what makes the result trustworthy — if you change the image *and* the audience, you won't know which drove the change.

### The A/B testing process

1. **Form a hypothesis** — e.g., "A video ad will get a lower cost-per-lead than a static image."
2. **Choose ONE variable** — creative, headline, audience, placement, or CTA.
3. **Define the success metric** — usually CPR or conversion rate, not just CTR.
4. **Split the audience evenly** so each version gets fair, non-overlapping exposure.
5. **Run long enough** — let it gather data (often 4–7 days) and reach enough conversions before judging.
6. **Pick a winner with confidence**, then scale it and test the next variable.

## Running tests on the platforms

- **Meta Ads**: Use the **A/B Test tool** (Experiments) in Ads Manager. It splits audiences so they don't overlap and declares a winner with a confidence level. You can test creative, audience, placement, or delivery optimization.
- **Google Ads**: Use **Experiments** (Drafts & Experiments) for Search/Display, or test ad variations within an ad group. Responsive Search Ads also auto-test asset combinations.

## Avoiding common mistakes

- **Don't judge too early.** Early data is noisy; wait for volume and exit the learning phase.
- **Don't change multiple variables at once.**
- **Don't optimize for vanity metrics.** A high CTR that doesn't convert wastes money.
- **Beware tiny sample sizes** — a 'winner' from 8 clicks isn't real.
- **Account for the learning phase** on Meta (roughly 50 conversions per ad set).

## A weekly optimization routine

1. Check spend pacing and CPR vs. target.
2. Pause clearly losing ads (enough data, far worse CPR).
3. Scale winners gradually (raise budget ~20% at a time).
4. Launch the next A/B test from your backlog of ideas.
5. Log learnings so you build a library of what works.

dm-m3-l01-keyword-research-search-intent.title: Keyword Research & Search Intent
objectives: Define keywords, search volume, keyword difficulty, and long-tail keywords
Identify the four types of search intent (informational, navigational, commercial, transactional)
Use free and freemium tools (Google autocomplete, Keyword Planner, AnswerThePublic, Google Trends) to
dm-m3-l01-keyword-research-search-intent.body:
## What Is a Keyword?

A **keyword** is the word or phrase a person types (or speaks) into a search engine. In digital marketing we use keywords to understand what audiences want and to make sure our content and ads appear when they search.

Key terms you must know:

- **Search volume** — roughly how many times a keyword is searched per month.
- **Keyword difficulty (KD)** — how hard it is to rank on page one (higher = more competition).
- **Long-tail keyword** — a longer, more specific phrase (e.g. *"vegan running shoes for flat feet"*). Lower volume but easier to rank and higher intent.
- **Head term** — a short, broad keyword (e.g. *"shoes"*). High volume, very competitive, vague intent.

## Search Intent: The Heart of Modern SEO

Google rewards content that matches **why** someone is searching, not just the words they use. There are four core intent types:

| Intent | What the user wants | Example query |
|---|---|---|
| **Informational** | To learn something | "how to tie a tie" |
| **Navigational** | To reach a specific site/brand | "netflix login" |
| **Commercial** | To research before buying | "best budget laptops 2024" |
| **Transactional** | To take action / buy now | "buy iphone 15 case" |

**Why it matters:** If you write a blog post for a transactional keyword, you'll lose to product pages. Match the content *type* to the intent.

## A Simple Keyword Research Workflow

1. **Seed keywords** — brainstorm 5–10 core topics for the business.
2. **Expand** — feed seeds into tools to get hundreds of related ideas.
3. **Pull data** — note volume and difficulty for each.
4. **Classify intent** — label every keyword I/N/C/T.
5. **Cluster** — group keywords by topic + intent.
6. **Prioritise** — pick targets using value vs. effort.

## Free & Freemium Tools

- **Google autocomplete & "People also ask"** — free idea generators built into search.
- **Google Keyword Planner** — free with a Google Ads account; gives volume ranges and ad competition.
- **Google Trends** — free; shows seasonality and rising terms.
- **AnswerThePublic** — freemium; surfaces question-based keywords (great for informational intent).
- **Ubersuggest / Keyword Surfer / Semrush (free tier)** — freemium; volume, difficulty, and related terms.

## Reading Intent From the SERP

The fastest way to confirm intent: **search the keyword yourself** and look at what ranks.

- Lots of blog posts/guides → informational
- Product or category pages, shopping ads → transactional/commercial
- A brand's homepage → navigational

If the top results are all product pages, don't try to rank a blog post there.

## Prioritising Keywords (Value vs. Effort)

Score each keyword on:

- **Value** — relevance to the business + intent (transactional often = higher value).
- **Effort** — keyword difficulty + how much content you'd need.

Target **low-difficulty, high-relevance** keywords first (quick wins), especially long-tail terms. Save high-volume head terms for long-term campaigns.

## Using Clusters for SEO and Ads

- **SEO:** Build one page per cluster (a "topic"), targeting the main keyword plus supporting long-tails.
- **Ads:** Group keywords into tight ad groups by intent so your ad copy matches the search — improving Quality Score and lowering cost.

## Key Takeaways

- Keywords reveal demand; intent reveals *how to serve it*.
- Always match content type to intent.
- Use free tools first — you can do excellent research for £0.
- Long-tail + low difficulty = best early wins.

dm-m3-l02-on-page-seo-fundamentals.title: On-Page SEO Fundamentals
objectives: Explain what on-page SEO is and how it differs from off-page and technical SEO
Write keyword-optimized title tags and meta descriptions that improve rankings and click-through rate
Structure page content using a logical heading hierarchy (H1–H3) and SEO-friendly URLs
Apply keyword research basics and place keywords naturally to match search intent
Optimize images with descriptive file names and alt text, and use internal links effectively
Run a simple on-page SEO audit using a repeatable checklist
dm-m3-l02-on-page-seo-fundamentals.body:
## What Is On-Page SEO?

**On-page SEO** is the practice of optimizing individual web pages—both the content and the HTML source code—so they rank higher in search engines and earn more relevant traffic. It's different from:

- **Off-page SEO** — actions taken *outside* your site (backlinks, mentions, social signals).
- **Technical SEO** — site speed, crawlability, mobile-friendliness, structured data.

As a Junior Social Media / Digital Marketing Assistant, on-page SEO is the part you can most directly influence when you create or edit content.

## Why It Matters

Search engines need to understand *what your page is about* and *who it's for*. On-page signals help them do that. Good on-page SEO also improves the **user experience** and **click-through rate (CTR)** from the search results page (SERP).

## The Core On-Page Elements

### 1. Title Tag
The clickable headline shown in search results and browser tabs.

- Keep it roughly **50–60 characters** so it doesn't get cut off.
- Put the **primary keyword near the front**.
- Make it compelling and unique for every page.
- Add your brand at the end when there's room.

```html
<title>Beginner's Guide to On-Page SEO | Acme Marketing</title>
```

### 2. Meta Description
A short summary (not a direct ranking factor, but it drives clicks).

- Aim for **120–155 characters**.
- Include the keyword and a clear benefit or call-to-action.
- Write it like an ad: make people want to click.

```html
<meta name="description" content="Learn on-page SEO basics: optimize titles, meta descriptions, headings, and content to rank higher. A practical checklist for beginners.">
```

### 3. Headings (H1–H6)
Headings structure content for readers and search engines.

- Use **one H1** per page (usually the main page heading/topic).
- Use **H2s** for main sections and **H3s** for sub-points.
- Include keywords naturally—don't force them.

### 4. URL Slug
- Keep URLs short, lowercase, and readable.
- Separate words with hyphens.
- Include the keyword; avoid dates, IDs, and stop words where possible.
- Good: `/blog/on-page-seo-guide` — Bad: `/blog/p?id=4821&cat=12`

### 5. Content & Keywords
- Start with **keyword research**: find terms your audience searches for (use Google autocomplete, 'People also ask', or a keyword tool).
- Match **search intent** — is the searcher looking to learn, compare, or buy?
- Use the primary keyword in the title, H1, first 100 words, and naturally throughout.
- Add related/secondary keywords and synonyms.
- **Avoid keyword stuffing** — write for humans first.

### 6. Images
- Use descriptive **file names** (`on-page-seo-checklist.jpg`, not `IMG_2931.jpg`).
- Add **alt text** describing the image (helps accessibility and image search).
- Compress images so they load fast.

### 7. Internal Links
- Link to other relevant pages on your site using **descriptive anchor text**.
- Helps users navigate and spreads ranking value across pages.

## A Simple On-Page SEO Workflow

1. Pick **one primary keyword** per page.
2. Write a unique **title tag** (~55 chars, keyword near front).
3. Write a click-worthy **meta description** (~150 chars).
4. Set a clear **H1** and logical H2/H3 structure.
5. Create a clean **URL slug**.
6. Write helpful content that satisfies search intent.
7. Optimize **images** (file names + alt text).
8. Add **internal links** with descriptive anchors.
9. Review on mobile and proofread.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- Duplicate or missing title tags.
- Stuffing keywords unnaturally.
- Multiple H1s or skipping heading levels for styling.
- Thin content that doesn't answer the query.
- Generic alt text like 'image1'.

## Key Takeaway

On-page SEO is about clearly communicating your page's topic to both **search engines and people**. Master the checklist and apply it every time you publish or edit a page.

dm-m3-l03-measuring-traffic-with-google-.title: Measuring Traffic with Google Analytics 4
objectives: Explain what GA4 is and how its event-based data model differs from older Universal Analytics
Create a GA4 property and install the tracking tag on a website
'Navigate the main GA4 report areas: Reports, Acquisition, Engagement, and Real-time'
Identify traffic sources and channels using the Acquisition reports
Set up and read conversions (key events) to measure goal completions
Read and interpret key metrics like users, sessions, engagement rate, and bounce
dm-m3-l03-measuring-traffic-with-google-.body:
## Why Google Analytics 4 Matters

As a junior digital marketing assistant, one of your core jobs is answering the question: *"Is our marketing actually working?"* Google Analytics 4 (GA4) is the free tool most businesses use to answer that question. It tells you how many people visit a website, where they came from, what they do once they arrive, and whether they complete the actions that matter (buying, signing up, contacting).

GA4 is the current version of Google Analytics, replacing the older Universal Analytics (UA), which stopped collecting data in July 2023. If you see tutorials mentioning "bounce rate" as the main metric or "Goals," they may be outdated — GA4 works differently.

## The Event-Based Data Model

The biggest change in GA4 is that **everything is an event**. In old Universal Analytics, data was organized around sessions and pageviews. In GA4, every interaction — a page view, a scroll, a click, a video play, a purchase — is recorded as an *event*.

- **Event**: something a user does (e.g. `page_view`, `scroll`, `click`, `session_start`).
- **Parameters**: extra detail attached to an event (e.g. which page, which link).
- **Key events (conversions)**: events you mark as especially important because they represent business goals.

This model lets GA4 track users across both websites and apps, and it is built with privacy and cookieless tracking in mind.

## Setting Up GA4

1. **Create a Google Analytics account** at analytics.google.com.
2. **Create a property** — a property holds the data for one website or app.
3. **Create a data stream** — for a website, choose "Web" and enter the site URL. GA4 generates a **Measurement ID** (looks like `G-XXXXXXXXXX`).
4. **Install the tag** on the website. Two common ways:
   - Paste the **Google tag (gtag.js)** snippet into the `<head>` of every page.
   - Use **Google Tag Manager (GTM)** to deploy the tag without editing code.
5. **Verify** data is flowing using the **Real-time** report — open the site in another tab and watch your visit appear.

GA4 automatically collects some events out of the box (called **Enhanced Measurement**): page views, scrolls, outbound clicks, site search, and file downloads.

## Key Reports You'll Use Daily

### Real-time
Shows who is on the site right now. Great for confirming a campaign launch or that tracking works.

### Acquisition
Answers *"Where did our traffic come from?"* It groups visitors into **channels**:
- **Organic Search** — from search engines like Google (unpaid).
- **Direct** — typed the URL or used a bookmark.
- **Organic Social** — from social media posts (unpaid).
- **Paid Search / Paid Social** — from ads.
- **Referral** — links from other websites.
- **Email** — from email campaigns (when tagged correctly).

### Engagement
Shows what people do: which pages they view, how long they stay, and which events fire.

### Monetization / Conversions
Shows revenue and key events (conversions) like form submissions or purchases.

## Key Metrics Explained

- **Users**: the number of distinct people who visited.
- **Sessions**: visits (one user can have several sessions).
- **Engaged sessions**: sessions lasting 10+ seconds, with a conversion, or 2+ page views.
- **Engagement rate**: % of sessions that were engaged. (GA4's healthier replacement for the old bounce rate.)
- **Bounce rate** (in GA4): the opposite of engagement rate — % of sessions that were *not* engaged.
- **Average engagement time**: how long users actively focused on the site.

## Setting Up Conversions (Key Events)

In GA4, you turn an important event into a conversion by marking it as a **key event**:
1. Go to **Admin → Events** (or **Data display → Events**).
2. Find the event (e.g. `generate_lead`, `purchase`, or a custom event).
3. Toggle **"Mark as key event."**

Now GA4 will count and report each time that action happens, so you can measure goal completions and conversion rates by channel.

## Using UTM Parameters

To make sure GA4 correctly attributes traffic from your campaigns, add **UTM parameters** to your links. Example:

`https://example.com/?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=spring_sale`

- `utm_source` — where it came from (instagram).
- `utm_medium` — the type of channel (social, email, cpc).
- `utm_campaign` — the campaign name.

These feed straight into the Acquisition reports so you can credit the right channel.

## Practical Tips

- Always check the **date range** in the top corner before reading any report.
- Compare periods (e.g. this month vs last month) to spot trends.
- Don't panic over single-day spikes — look at patterns over time.
- Use **Explore** for custom analysis once you're comfortable with standard reports.

dm-m3-l04-social-media-analytics-reporti.title: Social Media Analytics & Reporting
objectives: Identify the key metrics native platform analytics provide (reach, engagement, impressions, clicks,
dm-m3-l04-social-media-analytics-reporti.body:
## Why Social Media Analytics Matter

Posting content without measuring results is guessing. Analytics tell you what your audience actually responds to, whether you are moving toward business goals, and where to spend your time next. As a junior assistant, your job is often to **gather the numbers and present them clearly** so the team can make decisions.

## Core Metrics You Need to Know

- **Reach** — the number of unique accounts that saw your content.
- **Impressions** — the total number of times content was displayed (one person can create several impressions).
- **Engagement** — interactions: likes, comments, shares, saves, clicks.
- **Engagement rate** — engagement relative to reach or followers, expressed as a percentage.
- **Clicks / link clicks** — taps on a link, profile, or call-to-action.
- **Click-through rate (CTR)** — clicks divided by impressions.
- **Follower growth** — net new followers over a period.
- **Conversions** — a desired action completed (sign-up, purchase, download), tracked with UTM links or pixels.
- **Video views / watch time / completion rate** — for video-first platforms.

## Vanity vs Actionable Metrics

A **vanity metric** looks impressive but does not guide decisions on its own (e.g. raw follower count or total impressions). An **actionable metric** ties to a goal and informs next steps (e.g. engagement rate on link posts, CTR to the website, cost per conversion). Always ask: *"So what? What would I do differently because of this number?"*

## Key Formulas

```
Engagement rate (by reach) = (total engagements ÷ reach) × 100
CTR = (link clicks ÷ impressions) × 100
Follower growth rate = (net new followers ÷ starting followers) × 100
Conversion rate = (conversions ÷ clicks) × 100
```

## Where to Find the Data (Native Tools)

- **Instagram** — Professional Dashboard / Insights: reach, interactions, follower demographics, top content.
- **Facebook** — Meta Business Suite Insights: reach, engagement, page views.
- **LinkedIn** — Page Analytics: impressions, engagement rate, follower demographics by job title/industry.
- **TikTok** — Analytics tab: video views, watch time, traffic source, follower activity times.
- **X (Twitter)** — Analytics: impressions, engagements, top tweets.
- **YouTube** — YouTube Studio: views, watch time, audience retention.

Native analytics are free and accurate but only cover one platform at a time. Export to a spreadsheet to compare and track trends over time.

## Building a Clear Performance Report

A good report is short, visual and decision-focused. A reliable structure:

1. **Summary / TL;DR** — 2-3 sentences: what happened this period.
2. **Goals & KPIs** — what you were aiming for and the targets.
3. **Results** — key metrics vs last period and vs goal, with simple charts.
4. **Top performing content** — 2-3 posts and *why* they worked.
5. **Underperformers / learnings** — what flopped and the lesson.
6. **Next steps / recommendations** — 3-5 concrete actions.

### Tips for Reporting
- Always compare to a benchmark: previous period, goal, or industry average. A number alone is meaningless.
- Use percentages and trends (▲ +12%) not just raw totals.
- Round sensibly and keep charts simple.
- Write for a busy reader — lead with the takeaway, then the detail.
- End every report with **what you will do next**.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- Reporting impressions without context or comparison.
- Mixing date ranges across platforms.
- Drowning the report in every available metric — pick the ones tied to goals.
- Forgetting to explain *why* something performed well so it can be repeated.

dm-m4-l01-email-marketing-strategy-list-.title: Email Marketing Strategy & List Building
objectives: Explain why permission-based email marketing outperforms purchased or scraped lists
Map a basic email marketing funnel from awareness to conversion and retention
Design a compelling lead magnet that attracts the right subscribers
Build high-converting opt-in forms and landing pages with strong calls to action
Plan a welcome email sequence that nurtures new subscribers
Apply key list-building metrics and stay compliant with GDPR/CAN-SPAM rules
dm-m4-l01-email-marketing-strategy-list-.body:
## Why Email Marketing Still Wins

Email consistently delivers one of the highest returns on investment in digital marketing — often quoted around $36 for every $1 spent. Unlike social media followers, your email list is an asset you **own**: no algorithm decides who sees your message. For a junior marketing assistant, mastering email is a core, employable skill.

The golden rule is **permission**. You only email people who have actively asked to hear from you. Buying or scraping lists damages deliverability, breaks the law in many regions, and erodes trust.

## The Email Marketing Funnel

Think of email as guiding people through stages:

1. **Awareness** — A stranger discovers your brand (social post, blog, ad).
2. **Capture** — They give you their email in exchange for value (a lead magnet).
3. **Nurture** — A welcome sequence builds trust and educates.
4. **Convert** — Targeted offers turn subscribers into customers.
5. **Retain** — Ongoing newsletters and re-engagement keep them loyal.

Each stage needs its own content and goal. Don't ask for a sale before you've earned attention.

## Lead Magnets: The Trade of Value

People won't hand over their email for nothing. A **lead magnet** is a free, instantly useful resource offered in exchange for an email address. Good lead magnets are:

- **Specific** — solve one clear problem (e.g. "7-Day Instagram Content Calendar").
- **Quick to consume** — checklists, templates, mini-guides, discount codes.
- **Relevant** — attract your ideal subscriber, not just freebie hunters.
- **Instant** — delivered automatically right after sign-up.

Examples: checklists, templates, ebooks, webinars, free trials, discount codes, quizzes.

## Opt-In Forms & Landing Pages

Where you collect emails matters. Common placements: pop-ups, inline blog forms, footer bars, and dedicated **landing pages**.

A high-converting form has:

- A benefit-driven headline (what they get, not "Subscribe").
- Minimal fields — usually just an email (every extra field lowers conversion).
- A clear, action-oriented button ("Send me the checklist").
- Trust signals — privacy note, no spam promise.

Use **single opt-in** (subscribed immediately) for speed or **double opt-in** (confirm via email) for cleaner, more engaged lists and better compliance.

## The Welcome Sequence

New subscribers are most engaged in the first 48 hours. Automate a short welcome sequence:

1. **Email 1 (instant):** Deliver the lead magnet, set expectations.
2. **Email 2 (day 2):** Share your story / best content, build connection.
3. **Email 3 (day 4):** Soft offer or invitation to engage.

## Compliance Essentials

- **GDPR (EU):** Requires clear consent, easy unsubscribe, and data transparency.
- **CAN-SPAM (US):** Requires a physical address, honest subject lines, and a working unsubscribe link.
- Always include an unsubscribe option and never hide it.

## Metrics to Watch

- **List growth rate** — net new subscribers over time.
- **Conversion rate** of opt-in forms (visitors who subscribe).
- **Open rate** and **click-through rate** of emails.
- **Unsubscribe / spam rate** — early warning of poor relevance.

Track these in tools like Mailchimp, MailerLite, or ConvertKit, which most junior roles will expect you to use.

dm-m4-l02-building-automated-campaigns-i.title: Building Automated Campaigns in Mailchimp
objectives: Set up a Mailchimp audience and import or collect subscriber contacts correctly
Create audience segments and tags to target the right people with relevant messages
Build a multi-email automated welcome sequence using Mailchimp's Customer Journey builder
Write effective subject lines and email content that improve open and click rates
Measure and interpret open rate, click-through rate (CTR), and other key metrics
Apply A/B testing and list-hygiene best practices to improve campaign results
dm-m4-l02-building-automated-campaigns-i.body:
## Why Email Automation Matters

Email remains one of the highest-ROI channels in digital marketing, often returning far more per pound spent than paid social. Automation lets you send the right message to the right person at the right time *without* manually pressing send. As a Junior Social Media Assistant, you'll often own the welcome series, newsletters, and promotional sends.

**Automation** = pre-built email sequences triggered by a subscriber action (e.g. signing up, clicking a link, abandoning a cart).

## Key Mailchimp Concepts

- **Audience (List):** Your central database of contacts. Most small brands use a single audience and organise people inside it.
- **Tags:** Manual or automated labels you attach to contacts (e.g. `webinar-signup`, `VIP`).
- **Segments:** Saved filters based on conditions (e.g. "opened last 3 emails" or "located in London").
- **Customer Journey:** Mailchimp's visual automation builder where you set a *starting point* (trigger) and add *steps* (emails, delays, conditions).
- **Merge tags:** Personalisation placeholders like `*|FNAME|*` that insert a subscriber's first name.

## Step 1 — Set Up Your Audience

1. Go to **Audience > All contacts**.
2. Add a signup form or import contacts (CSV). Only import people who **opted in** — this is a legal requirement under GDPR/CAN-SPAM.
3. Collect at minimum: email address, first name, and signup source.

## Step 2 — Segment Your Audience

Don't blast everyone the same message. Create segments such as:

- **New subscribers** (joined in last 7 days)
- **Engaged** (opened or clicked recently)
- **Inactive** (no opens in 90 days — candidates for a re-engagement email)

Segments make emails more relevant, which lifts open and click rates and reduces unsubscribes.

## Step 3 — Build an Automated Welcome Sequence

Use **Automations > Customer Journey > Build from scratch**.

A simple 3-email welcome journey:

1. **Trigger:** Contact joins audience / signup form submitted.
2. **Email 1 (immediately):** Warm welcome + what to expect.
3. **Delay:** Wait 2 days.
4. **Email 2:** Share your best content or a brand story.
5. **Delay:** Wait 3 days.
6. **Email 3:** Offer or call-to-action (discount code, free resource).

Add **if/else branches** to send different content based on whether someone opened Email 1.

## Step 4 — Write Emails That Convert

- **Subject line:** Short (under ~50 characters), curiosity or value-driven. This drives open rate.
- **Preview text:** The snippet after the subject — reinforce the subject.
- **Personalisation:** Use `*|FNAME|*` to greet by name.
- **One clear CTA:** A single, obvious button drives click-through rate.
- **Mobile-friendly:** Over half of emails are opened on phones — keep it scannable.

## Step 5 — Measure Performance

Key metrics in the campaign report:

- **Open Rate** = (unique opens ÷ emails delivered) × 100. Typical benchmark ~20–35%.
- **Click-Through Rate (CTR)** = (unique clicks ÷ emails delivered) × 100. Typical benchmark ~2–5%.
- **Bounce rate:** Undeliverable emails — high bounces hurt your sender reputation.
- **Unsubscribe rate:** If high, your content or frequency may be off.

> Note: Apple Mail Privacy Protection inflates open rates, so treat clicks as the more reliable engagement signal.

## Step 6 — Optimise with A/B Testing

Mailchimp lets you test variables like subject line, send time, or content. Send each version to a sample, and the winner (by opens or clicks) goes to the rest of the list. Test **one variable at a time**.

## List Hygiene Best Practices

- Remove or re-engage inactive contacts regularly.
- Always include an unsubscribe link (legally required).
- Never buy email lists — it damages deliverability and breaks the law.

## Capstone Tie-In

For your portfolio, document a complete automated welcome journey: include a screenshot of the Customer Journey map, your three email drafts, the segment you targeted, and a short report explaining the open/click results and what you'd improve.

dm-m4-l03-integrated-capstone-a-full-mul.title: Integrated Capstone: A Full Multi-Channel Campaign
objectives: Define a single SMART business goal and tie every channel back to it
Map the customer journey across ads, content, SEO, and email
Build a coordinated campaign calendar with consistent messaging and creative
Set up tracking with UTM parameters and channel-specific KPIs
Assemble the campaign into a professional capstone portfolio case study
dm-m4-l03-integrated-capstone-a-full-mul.body:
## Why Integrated Campaigns Matter

Real businesses rarely succeed with a single channel. A customer might see an Instagram ad, read a blog post, find you again through Google, and finally convert after an email. An **integrated multi-channel campaign** coordinates ads, organic content, SEO, and email so they reinforce one another around a single goal. This capstone proves you can think like a marketer, not just operate one tool.

## Step 1: Start With One Business Goal

Everything begins with a single, measurable objective. Use the SMART framework:

- **Specific**: Generate newsletter sign-ups for a new product launch
- **Measurable**: 500 new subscribers
- **Achievable**: based on current traffic and budget
- **Relevant**: tied to revenue or growth
- **Time-bound**: within 4 weeks

Write this as one sentence: *"Acquire 500 new email subscribers for the spring collection launch in 4 weeks on a $400 ad budget."* Every channel decision must serve this goal.

## Step 2: Map the Customer Journey

Think in stages and assign channels to each:

| Stage | Goal | Channels |
|-------|------|----------|
| Awareness | Reach new people | Paid social ads, organic posts |
| Consideration | Build interest/trust | Blog content, SEO landing page |
| Conversion | Capture the lead | Lead-gen form, opt-in offer |
| Retention | Nurture & sell | Email welcome series |

Notice how channels hand off to each other. An ad drives traffic to an SEO-optimized landing page; the page offers a lead magnet; the email series nurtures the subscriber.

## Step 3: Create a Consistent Message & Creative

Define one **core message** and one **visual identity** that appears everywhere:

- Same value proposition headline across ad, landing page, and email
- Same colors, fonts, and hero image
- Same call-to-action verb ("Get early access")

Consistency builds recognition and trust as users move between channels.

## Step 4: Build the Campaign Calendar

Sequence activity over the 4 weeks:

- **Week 1**: Publish SEO blog post + landing page; warm-up organic posts
- **Week 2**: Launch paid social ads driving to landing page
- **Week 3**: Retarget engagers; send first email to new subscribers
- **Week 4**: Final push ads + last-chance email; measure

## Step 5: Track Everything With UTMs

UTM parameters tell you which channel drove each result in Google Analytics.

`https://site.com/spring?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=spring_launch`

- **utm_source** = where (instagram, google, newsletter)
- **utm_medium** = type (cpc, organic, email)
- **utm_campaign** = which campaign (spring_launch)

Use a consistent naming convention so reports stay clean.

## Step 6: Measure With Channel KPIs

- **Ads**: CTR, CPC, cost per acquisition (CPA)
- **Content/SEO**: organic sessions, time on page, keyword ranking
- **Email**: open rate, click rate, conversion rate
- **Overall**: total subscribers vs. 500 goal, blended CPA

## Step 7: Package as a Portfolio Case Study

Document the campaign as a story: the goal, your strategy, the channel plan, screenshots of assets, the results (or projected results), and what you learned. This case study is the centerpiece of your job application — it shows end-to-end thinking.

dm-m4-l04-building-your-portfolio-landin.title: Building Your Portfolio & Landing the Job
objectives: Select and organize your strongest campaign work into a professional portfolio that proves real skills
Write portfolio case studies using a clear problem–action–result structure with metrics
Tailor your resume and LinkedIn profile to junior digital marketing job descriptions using keywords
dm-m4-l04-building-your-portfolio-landin.body:
## Why a Portfolio Matters for Junior Marketers

Entry-level marketing is competitive, and employers rarely hire on a degree alone. They want **proof you can do the work**: plan a campaign, create content, read analytics, and communicate results. A portfolio turns your bootcamp projects into evidence. Even if your work was a practice or capstone project, presenting it professionally shows initiative and skill.

> Rule of thumb: *Show, don't just tell.* A screenshot of a real email open-rate report beats the phrase "familiar with email marketing."

## What to Include in a Marketing Portfolio

Aim for **3–5 strong pieces** rather than everything you've made. Quality and clarity win.

- **Email campaign** — subject lines, the email design, audience, and the results (open rate, click rate).
- **Social media content** — sample posts, a content calendar, and engagement numbers.
- **Analytics snapshot** — a screenshot or summary showing you can read data (Google Analytics, Meta Insights, Mailchimp reports).
- **A short strategy doc** — goals, target audience, channels, and KPIs for one project.
- **Capstone case study** — your full project tying it all together.

For practice projects, label them clearly (e.g., "Mock campaign for a local coffee shop") so you're honest while still showcasing skill.

## The Case Study Formula (Problem → Action → Result)

Each portfolio piece should tell a quick story:

1. **Context / Problem** — "A small bakery wanted to grow their email list and drive weekend sales."
2. **Goal & Strategy** — "Goal: 200 new subscribers in 4 weeks. Strategy: a 10% discount lead magnet promoted on Instagram."
3. **Action** — what you actually did: wrote the emails, designed the signup form, built the automation.
4. **Result** — the numbers: "32% open rate (industry avg ~21%), 140 new subscribers, 12 redemptions."
5. **Reflection** — what you learned or would improve next time.

Always include **metrics**, and add context so numbers mean something (compare to averages or starting points).

## Where to Host Your Portfolio

You don't need to be a web developer. Use a free or low-cost tool:

- **Notion** — fast, clean, easy to share with a link.
- **Canva** — design a PDF or simple website.
- **Carrd / Wix / Google Sites** — simple one-page sites.
- **PDF** — a polished document you can attach to applications.

Make sure it's **mobile-friendly**, loads fast, and has a clear way to contact you.

## Tailoring Your Resume

Recruiters skim resumes in seconds, and many companies use **Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS)** that scan for keywords.

- **Mirror the job description.** If it says "email marketing, content creation, Google Analytics," use those exact terms (truthfully).
- **Lead with achievements, not duties.** Use the formula: *action verb + what you did + result/metric.*
  - Weak: "Responsible for social media posts."
  - Strong: "Created and scheduled 30+ Instagram posts, growing engagement 18% over 6 weeks."
- **Include a skills section** with tools: Mailchimp, Canva, Meta Business Suite, Google Analytics, Hootsuite.
- **Add your portfolio link** at the top near your contact info.
- Keep it to **one page** for entry level.

## Optimize LinkedIn

- Professional headshot and a headline that says what you do: "Junior Digital Marketer | Email & Social Media | Open to work."
- A short **About** summary with your focus and portfolio link.
- Add your bootcamp, projects, and skills. Turn on the **Open to Work** setting.

## Acing the Interview with STAR

Use the **STAR method** for behavioral questions:

- **S**ituation — set the scene briefly.
- **T**ask — what needed to be done.
- **A**ction — what *you* did.
- **R**esult — the outcome, with a metric if possible.

Common junior marketing questions to prepare:

- "Walk me through a campaign you're proud of." (Use your capstone.)
- "How do you measure success on social media?" (Mention KPIs: reach, engagement rate, CTR, conversions.)
- "What marketing tools have you used?"
- "How do you stay current with trends?"

Prepare 2–3 thoughtful questions to ask them, and follow up with a thank-you email within 24 hours.

## Quick Action Plan

1. Pick your 3–5 best pieces.
2. Write each as a Problem→Action→Result case study with metrics.
3. Build a Notion/Canva portfolio and grab the share link.
4. Tailor your resume and LinkedIn to a target job posting.
5. Practice STAR answers out loud.

g1-l01-how-llms-behave.title: How LLMs behave
objectives: Explain how text is split into tokens and why token count matters
Describe the context window and what happens when you exceed it
Explain next-token prediction as the core mechanism behind every response
Adjust temperature and top-p to control randomness in a deliberate way
Predict how a given setting will make outputs more focused or more varied
Connect token budgets to cost and latency in a production system
g1-l01-how-llms-behave.body:
## A model that only predicts the next token

A large language model does one thing astonishingly well: given some text, it predicts what token comes next. Everything else — answering questions, writing code, summarising a document — is that single trick repeated thousands of times. There is no database lookup, no hidden search engine. The model holds a learned sense of "what usually follows what" and uses it one step at a time.

This matters because it reframes how you think about prompting. You are not issuing a command to a program; you are giving the model a starting context and letting it continue in the most probable way. Good prompts shape that probability.

## Tokens: the unit the model actually sees

Models do not read characters or words directly. They read **tokens** — chunks of text mapped to integers. A token is often a whole common word, but longer or rarer words get split into word-pieces. As a rough rule for English, one token is about 3 to 4 characters, or roughly three-quarters of a word.

This is why `cat` might be one token but `unbelievability` is several, and why code or non-English text can tokenise very differently. You will count tokens often, because they drive cost and fit.

## The context window

The **context window** is the total number of tokens the model can attend to in a single request — your prompt *and* the response it generates, combined. Current Claude models such as Opus `claude-opus-4-8` and Sonnet `claude-sonnet-4-6` offer very large windows, but every model has a limit.

If you push past it, the model cannot see the overflow: older content gets truncated or the request is rejected. Treat the window as a budget. Long documents, long chat histories, and large tool outputs all compete for the same space.

## Next-token sampling: temperature and top-p

At each step the model produces a probability distribution over every possible next token. How you *pick* from that distribution decides how the text feels.

- **Temperature** reshapes the distribution. Low temperature sharpens it toward the single most likely token, giving focused, repeatable output. High temperature flattens it, so less likely tokens get a chance and the text becomes more varied — and more surprising.
- **Top-p** (nucleus sampling) trims the candidate pool. It keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to `p` (say 0.9) and samples from those, discarding the long tail of implausible options.

Use low temperature for extraction, classification, and anything you need to be deterministic-ish. Use higher temperature for brainstorming or creative drafts.

```bash
# Conceptually, per request you tune:
temperature = 0.0   # focused, near-deterministic
temperature = 1.0   # varied, creative
top_p       = 0.9   # ignore the unlikely tail
```

A note for later: some current Claude models remove `temperature` and `top_p` entirely and steer behaviour through prompting and effort instead. The *concept* still explains how any LLM turns predictions into words — and that intuition transfers to every provider you will meet, including the models you can run on Amazon Bedrock or Azure.

## Why this is foundational

Once you internalise "tokenise, predict, sample, repeat," the rest of the course clicks into place. Hallucination, cost, latency, and the value of structure all follow from this one loop.

## Your task

Take a short paragraph of your own writing and estimate its token count (about words divided by 0.75). Then write one sentence describing what you would expect a low-temperature versus a high-temperature continuation of that paragraph to look like.

g1-l02-where-llms-fail.title: Where LLMs fail
objectives: Define hallucination and explain why next-token prediction produces it
Explain knowledge cutoff and why models are stale on recent facts
Describe why raw LLMs are unreliable at arithmetic and long multi-step logic
Match each failure mode to a concrete mitigation pattern
Decide when to add retrieval, tools, or verification to a system
Treat model output as untrusted input that needs validation
g1-l02-where-llms-fail.body:
## Failures are predictable, not random

In the last lesson you saw that an LLM only predicts the next most-plausible token. That single mechanism explains its strengths *and* its three classic failure modes. Once you can name each one and explain why it happens, you can engineer around it. None of this means the models are bad — it means you treat them like any component with known limits.

## Hallucination

A **hallucination** is a confident statement that is simply not true: a fake citation, an invented API method, a plausible-but-wrong fact. It happens because the model optimises for *plausibility*, not truth. If the most fluent continuation of your prompt is a made-up function name, the model will happily produce it — with the same calm tone it uses for correct answers.

The danger is the confidence. There is no built-in "I don't know" unless the prompt and training encourage it. Mitigations:

- **Ground the model** in real source text (retrieval-augmented generation), and ask it to answer *only* from that text and cite it.
- **Give it permission to say "I don't know"** explicitly in the system prompt.
- **Verify** anything load-bearing — links, numbers, names — with a second check.

## Knowledge cutoff and recency

A model is trained on data up to a **cutoff date**. After that date it knows nothing — not last week's release, not today's prices, not the incident you are debugging right now. Ask about a recent event and it will either admit ignorance or, worse, hallucinate a plausible-sounding answer.

This is not a bug you can prompt away; the information is genuinely absent. The fix is to **bring the data to the model**: retrieve relevant documents and put them in the context window, or give the model a **web search / fetch tool** so it can pull current information itself. As a cloud engineer you already think this way — you wouldn't expect a cached value to reflect a change that happened after it was cached.

## Weak arithmetic and multi-step logic

LLMs are surprisingly shaky at exact arithmetic and long chains of reasoning. Multiply two large numbers and a raw model often produces something *close* but wrong. The reason is the same prediction loop: it pattern-matches digit tokens rather than executing an exact algorithm, and small errors compound across many steps.

The mitigations are pragmatic:

- **Offload the calculation** to a tool — a calculator or a code-execution sandbox — and have the model call it. Deterministic code gives an exact answer every time.
- **Encourage step-by-step reasoning** for logic problems so the model breaks a hard task into smaller, checkable pieces.
- **Verify the result** when correctness matters.

```text
Bad:  "What is 48273 * 1956?"  -> model guesses a close-but-wrong number
Good: model calls a calculator tool -> exact result, every time
```

## The unifying mindset

Notice the pattern across all three: the fix is rarely "prompt harder." It is to **add structure around the model** — grounding for hallucination, fresh data for recency, tools for math and logic — and to treat every output as untrusted input that earns trust only after validation. This is exactly the security-and-reliability instinct you already have. Modules 2 and beyond build directly on these mitigations.

## Your task

Write down a real question from your own work for each failure mode — one that would trigger a hallucination, one blocked by knowledge cutoff, and one requiring exact arithmetic — and note the single mitigation you would reach for in each case.

g1-l03-calling-the-api.title: Calling the API directly
objectives: Send a basic request to the Anthropic Messages API
Explain the roles user and assistant and how turns alternate
Use the top-level system parameter to set behaviour
Describe content blocks and why content is a list, not a string
'Read the key fields of a response: content, stop_reason, and usage'
Recognise the same request shape on Amazon Bedrock and Azure
g1-l03-calling-the-api.body:
## Start at the raw API, not a framework

It is tempting to reach straight for a high-level framework. Don't — not yet. Frameworks hide exactly the request shape you most need to understand. If you learn the **raw Messages API** first, every framework, agent loop, and abstraction you meet later becomes obvious, because you will recognise what it is generating underneath. This is the same reason you learned HTTP before learning a web framework.

Everything Anthropic does goes through one endpoint: `POST /v1/messages`. Tools, streaming, and structured output are all *features of this single endpoint*, not separate APIs. Master its shape and you have mastered the surface.

## The anatomy of a request

A request has a few core parts: the `model`, a `max_tokens` cap, an optional top-level `system` prompt, and a `messages` array.

```python
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a concise assistant for DevOps engineers.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "In one line, what is idempotency?"}
    ],
)
print(response.content[0].text)
```

Notice what is *not* here: no separate "prompt" string, no template engine. Just a model, a system instruction, and a conversation.

## Roles: user and assistant

The `messages` array is the conversation. Each entry has a `role` — either `user` (you) or `assistant` (the model) — and turns alternate. The first message must be `user`. To continue a conversation, you append the assistant's previous reply and your next `user` message, then send the whole history again. The API is **stateless**: it remembers nothing between calls, so you always send the full conversation.

The **system** prompt is deliberately *not* a role inside the array. It is a top-level `system` parameter that sets persona, rules, and context for the whole exchange. Keeping it separate makes its authority clear and its placement cache-friendly.

## Content blocks

Look closely at `content`. For a simple text turn you can pass a plain string, but under the hood content is a **list of typed blocks**. That is why `response.content[0].text` indexes into a list.

```python
messages = [{
    "role": "user",
    "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this diagram."},
        # an image block could go here too
    ],
}]
```

Blocks are the reason one message can mix text with an image, or carry a `tool_use` request, or return a `tool_result`. Every advanced feature in this module is just a new block type. Learn the container now and the features slot in later.

## Reading the response

The response object carries `content` (the list of output blocks), `stop_reason` (why it stopped — `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `tool_use`, `refusal`), and `usage` (input and output token counts — your cost meter). Always check `stop_reason` before assuming a turn is complete; in later lessons it is how you detect a tool call.

## The same shape, in your clouds

Here is the payoff for your background: this exact request shape runs on **Amazon Bedrock** and **Azure / Microsoft Foundry** too. The client setup and the model-id string change (Bedrock prefixes ids, for example `anthropic.claude-opus-4-8`), but `messages`, `system`, roles, and content blocks are identical. Learn it once here on the first-party API; deploy it wherever you already operate.

## Your task

Using the Anthropic Python SDK, send a single Messages request with a one-sentence `system` prompt of your choice and one `user` message. Print `response.content[0].text`, then also print `response.stop_reason` and `response.usage` and note what each tells you.

g1-l04-streaming.title: Streaming responses
objectives: Explain what server-sent events are and how a streamed response arrives
Consume incremental text deltas with the SDK streaming helper
Reassemble the full message from a stream when you need it
Decide when streaming is worth it and when it is not
Use streaming to avoid HTTP timeouts on long or large outputs
Identify the key stream event types in order
g1-l04-streaming.body:
## Why streaming exists

When you call the API normally, you wait for the model to finish, then receive the whole response at once. For a long answer that can mean staring at a blank screen for many seconds. **Streaming** changes the delivery: the response arrives incrementally, token by token, as it is generated. The user sees words appear in real time, exactly like a chat UI.

There is also a hard engineering reason. Very long generations can exceed an HTTP request's idle timeout — the connection sits silent while the model works, and a proxy or the SDK gives up. Streaming keeps data flowing, so the connection stays alive. In fact the SDKs will refuse a non-streaming request whose `max_tokens` is large enough to risk a timeout. For big outputs, streaming is not optional.

## Server-sent events

Streaming is delivered as **server-sent events (SSE)** — a simple one-way stream over a single HTTP response. The server writes a sequence of `event:` and `data:` lines, and your client reads them as they arrive. It is plain HTTP, not WebSockets, so it works through ordinary proxies and load balancers you already run.

```text
event: message_start
data: {"type":"message_start", ...}

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type":"content_block_delta","delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":"Hello"}}

event: message_stop
data: {"type":"message_stop"}
```

The key events, in order: `message_start` (metadata), one or more `content_block_start` / `content_block_delta` / `content_block_stop` sequences (the actual content), `message_delta` (carries the final `stop_reason` and usage), and `message_stop` at the very end.

## Consuming token deltas

The SDK gives you a streaming helper so you rarely parse raw SSE yourself. The simplest pattern iterates over text as it arrives:

```python
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a short poem about CI/CD."}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)
```

Each chunk is a **delta** — a small piece of new text. You `flush` so it appears immediately. That loop is the whole user-facing magic of a chat interface.

## Getting the final message

Often you want to stream for responsiveness *and* still have the complete object — full text, `stop_reason`, token usage — when it is done. The helpers accumulate that for you:

```python
with client.messages.stream(...) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)
    final = stream.get_final_message()
    print("\nTokens:", final.usage.output_tokens)
```

In TypeScript the equivalent is `stream.finalMessage()`. You get the live experience and the structured result without stitching deltas by hand.

## When to stream — and when not to

Stream when latency is **visible to a human** (chat, assistants, anything interactive) or when the output is **long enough to risk a timeout**. Skip streaming when you just need a short final result for a backend step — a one-word classification, a small extraction — where a single non-streaming call is simpler to write and read.

For your DevOps instincts: streaming is the difference between a CLI tool that feels alive and one that appears to hang. It is also your timeout insurance for any large generation.

## Your task

Write a small script that streams a response to a multi-paragraph prompt and prints the text as it arrives. Then call `get_final_message()` (or `finalMessage()`) and print the output token count and `stop_reason`.

g1-l05-structured-output.title: Structured / JSON output
objectives: Explain why parsing free-form prose for data is fragile
Request structured output by supplying a JSON schema
Use the SDK parse helper to validate output against a schema
Describe the difference between JSON output and strict tool use
Choose structured output when a downstream system needs reliable data
Handle the cases where structured output can still fail
g1-l05-structured-output.body:
## The problem with prose

A model loves to talk. Ask for someone's email and plan and it might say: "Sure! Jane Doe can be reached at jane@co.com and she's on the Enterprise plan." Lovely for a human. A nightmare for code. To extract the fields you would write a regex — and that regex breaks the instant the model phrases things differently next time: "Jane (jane@co.com) — Enterprise tier." Same data, new wording, broken parser.

This is the central lesson: **never build a production pipeline on parsing free-form prose.** Natural language has infinite valid phrasings, and your parser only handles the ones you have seen. You need the model to return data in a shape you define.

## Structured output: define the shape

The fix is **structured output**. You hand the API a **JSON schema** describing exactly the fields and types you want, and the response is constrained to match it. Instead of hoping for JSON, you require it.

```python
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Extract: Jane Doe (jane@co.com) wants Enterprise."}],
    output_config={
        "format": {
            "type": "json_schema",
            "schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "name":  {"type": "string"},
                    "email": {"type": "string"},
                    "plan":  {"type": "string"},
                },
                "required": ["name", "email", "plan"],
                "additionalProperties": False,
            },
        }
    },
)
```

The first content block is now reliable JSON you can `json.loads()` with confidence.

## The parse helper

Even better, the SDK can validate *and* type the result for you. In Python you define a Pydantic model and call `messages.parse`:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Contact(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: str
    plan: str

response = client.messages.parse(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}],
    output_format=Contact,
)
contact = response.parsed_output   # a validated Contact instance
print(contact.email)
```

No manual JSON handling, no regex, and an immediate type error if something is off. TypeScript does the same with a Zod schema.

## Structured output vs strict tool use

These are two flavours of the same idea — schema enforcement on the one Messages endpoint. **Structured output** (`output_config.format`) constrains the model's *response body*. **Strict tool use** (`strict: true` on a tool) constrains the *input parameters* of a tool the model calls. You will use the second in the next lesson. Both guarantee shape; they just apply it in different places.

## It is reliable, not magic

Structured output dramatically increases reliability, but it does not override everything. If the model **refuses** for safety (`stop_reason: "refusal"`) or the output is **cut off** by `max_tokens` mid-object, you can still get an incomplete or non-conforming result. So you keep validating and handle those cases — the same defensive posture you already apply to any external input. The first request with a new schema is also slightly slower while the schema compiles; later calls hit a cache.

## Why this matters for you

Every integration you build will hand model output to something else — a database, an API, a dashboard. Structured output is the contract that makes those handoffs safe. It turns a chatty model into a dependable component in a pipeline, which is exactly what an Applied GenAI Engineer ships.

## Your task

Define a small JSON schema (or Pydantic / Zod model) for a data record relevant to your work, then make a request that extracts that record from a sentence of prose. Parse the result and print one field, and note what would have broken if you had used a regex instead.

g1-l06-tool-calling.title: Tool (function) calling
objectives: Define a tool with a name, description, and input schema
Recognise a tool_use block and a stop_reason of tool_use
Execute the requested tool with the model's supplied input
Return a tool_result block tied to the matching tool_use id
Loop the conversation until the model produces a final answer
Explain why tool calling is the foundation of agents
g1-l06-tool-calling.body:
## Letting the model call your code

In lesson two you saw that models are weak at math and stuck behind a knowledge cutoff. **Tool calling** is the cure. You give the model a set of functions it may ask you to run — a calculator, a database lookup, a weather API — and when it needs one, it requests the call. *You* run the function and hand back the result, and the model uses it to finish its answer.

The critical detail: the model never executes anything itself. It only asks. Your code stays in control of what actually runs — which, for a security-minded engineer, is exactly the right boundary. This is the raw mechanism every agent framework is built on, so learn it here, directly.

## Defining a tool

A tool is a JSON object with three parts: a `name`, a `description` (the model reads this to decide *when* to use the tool — be clear and specific), and an `input_schema` describing the parameters as JSON schema.

```python
tools = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get the current weather for a city. Use when the user asks about weather.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string", "description": "City name"}},
        "required": ["city"],
    },
}]
```

Notice there is no code here — just a contract. The model decides whether and how to call it.

## The tool_use → tool_result loop
